articles.title_orig: How Nvidia’s billion-dollar turnaround in China is threatened by Huang’s exit
articles.title_zh: How Nvidia’s billion-dollar turnaround in China is threatened by Huang’s exit
articles.content_orig:
By Eduardo Baptista and Liam Mo
Nov 23 (Reuters) – Nvidia staged a comeback in China’s booming artificial-intelligence industry by selling less powerful chips and software after US export bans cost it billions in sales – but that business is now threatened by the scandal surrounding former CEO Jensen Huang.
Nvidia products used to run AI models powering everything from business software to humanoid robots have found growing demand in China from universities, companies and research institutes, even as the US chipmaker’s most advanced AI processors remain largely off limits, according to people in the industry and a Reuters review of more than 100 Chinese corporate disclosures and procurement records.
Now, after Huang’s abrupt resignation, some Chinese customers are cancelling or hesitating to place orders, jeopardizing billions in revenue, as US government scrutiny of Nvidia intensifies after Huang’s ​exit, people familiar with the matter said.
Huang left Nvidia earlier this month following reports of extramarital affairs, including one involving a businesswoman suspected by US authorities of spying for China. The co-founder and CEO, a close ally of US President Donald Trump, had been a ‌vigorous defender of chip sales to China and one of the industry’s most influential voices in Washington.
Before Huang’s troubles, revenue from customers headquartered in China and Hong Kong had more than tripled year over year, rising from $2.97 billion in Nvidia’s October 2025 quarter to $11.05 billion in the quarter ended October 25, 2026, according to the company’s financial results.
Even as the company was reporting growing China revenue, Huang publicly said that Washington’s restrictions had decimated the company’s chip business in China, and that the company’s share of China’s AI chip market had plunged to zero because of US restrictions.
China’s reliance on Nvidia is attracting attention in Washington and may attract more after Democrats routed Trump’s Republican Party in the November 3 midterm elections, winning control of the US House and Senate from January.
“Congress is going to press hard, on a bipartisan basis, on chips and chipmaking capabilities, after two years of close to zero oversight,” said Mike Kuiken, vice chair of the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission, a bipartisan organization that advises Congress.
CANCELLED ORDERS, UNSETTLED CUSTOMERS
Some Chinese customers have begun cancelling orders amid concerns that the ‌RTX PRO 5500 –  a ​graphics card designed for professional computers that can also run AI models – may not be permitted into China, according to two people familiar with the matter. Reuters could not determine the scale of the ⁠cancellations or whether the US or China would restrict shipments.
The controversy surrounding Huang has ⁠also deeply unsettled Chinese suppliers, customers and other partners whose businesses depend on Nvidia, according to two people familiar with the matter. They fear heightened scrutiny could extend to Nvidia’s remaining legal chip sales.
Before Huang’s departure, Chinese companies sought more than 6 million units of a new Nvidia graphics card, worth nearly $70 billion at listed prices, Reuters reported in October, citing people familiar with the matter. That’s more than twice the company’s expected worldwide production next year.
Unlike Nvidia’s most powerful chips, which are used in vast data centres to develop advanced AI models, the less powerful and cheaper products it sells in China are the company’s PC, gaming and robotics lines that can run existing AI models, generate images and video, analyse business data and help robots respond to their surroundings.
Nvidia’s directors launched an investigation into Huang’s ties to the woman on November 8 and said ​they had no reason to believe the company’s secrets or US national security were compromised. China denied the espionage allegations. Reuters has not independently verified the claims.
To replace Huang, Nvidia appointed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO.
When Washington began restricting Nvidia’s most powerful AI processors in 2022, the company developed weaker alternatives to comply with US rules. The first such chips drew strong demand but were soon banned by new US curbs.
One later product, the RTX PRO 6000D, which was designed for running AI models on professional computers, drew lukewarm demand from major Chinese technology companies after ⁠its introduction last year, Reuters previously reported.
But that changed early this year as AI computing power in China grew scarce. Many companies began using AI models across their businesses rather than ⁠simply developing them, while domestic chipmakers struggled to keep pace, according to three people familiar with the matter.
Even Huawei, Nvidia’s leading Chinese rival, acknowledged in September that it could not produce enough AI computing equipment to meet domestic ​demand.
Chinese domestic chip alternatives remain costly and difficult to adopt. Developers have spent years building software around Nvidia’s technology, making switching expensive, while shortages of advanced memory required to run AI chips have pushed up domestic chip prices.
Huawei and Cambricon raised prices for some AI chips by 20% to 50% in recent months, Reuters ​reported in September.
Cloud providers, technology companies, manufacturers and universities are consequently turning to Nvidia’s lower-powered products to run AI models, generate images, analyse data and automate tasks, according to the three people.
Demand has been particularly strong for its ‌RTX PRO 5500 graphics card, with Chinese orders exceeding 6 million units against expected global production of up to 3 million in 2027, Reuters reported last month.
Priced at about $11,400, the card is offered globally but was developed to meet Chinese demand, according to a person familiar with Nvidia’s planning.
Nvidia had observed Chinese companies obtaining its RTX 5090 gaming cards through unofficial channels and combining them into servers to run AI services, the person said.
Although designed for high-end gaming computers, the RTX 5090 is powerful enough to exceed US export limits. It can’t be sold in China because US export restrictions apply to a chip’s capabilities rather than whether it is marketed for gaming or AI.
The RTX PRO 5500 offers more memory and is intended for business AI applications. Nvidia asked Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co to shift some manufacturing capacity from the gaming card to the new product, according to two people familiar with its plans.
Nvidia had told some customers to expect samples in December ⁠and deliveries beginning in early 2027, the two people said.
Those plans now face fresh uncertainty, compounded by Beijing’s efforts to promote domestic chips. Large purchases of this new Nvidia chip by internet companies such as ByteDance and Alibaba could require Chinese government approval, according to two people familiar with the matter.
TSMC and China’s industry regulator did not respond to comment requests.
Nvidia’s influence extends beyond data centres into China’s fast-growing humanoid robot industry.
The company’s Jetson processors allow robots to interpret information from cameras and sensors and respond in real time, while its Isaac software helps engineers develop and test robots in virtual environments.
An ⁠analysis by the Jamestown Foundation, a US think tank, identified at least 14 Chinese companies using parts of Nvidia’s robotics ‌platform, including Unitree, XPeng Robotics, AgiBot and Fourier Intelligence.
Those robotics firms did not respond to comment requests.
A former Unitree employee said the company’s AI development relied heavily on Nvidia’s Jetson Nano and Orin processors, despite its emphasis ⁠on domestic innovation. Replacing them with Chinese alternatives such as Rockchip would be difficult because of their limited computing capabilities, the person said.

articles.title_orig: President Trump wants Jensen Huang back at Nvidia despite widening China spy probe
articles.title_zh: President Trump wants Jensen Huang back at Nvidia despite widening China spy probe
articles.content_orig:
By JAMES GORDON, US NEWS REPORTER
Published: 22:51 EST, 22 November 2026 | Updated: 00:27 EST, 23 November 2026
President Donald Trump urged Nvidia to immediately reinstate disgraced billionaire Jensen Huang as chief executive, insisting his return would be good not just for the technology giant but for the entire United States.
In a Truth Social posting on Sunday night, Trump publicly urged Nvidia's board of directors to reverse its decision to part ways with Huang following revelations about his extramarital affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of having links to Beijing 's intelligence services.
'I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang. It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A. President DONALD J. TRUMP,' the president wrote.
The president's appeal came despite Nvidia's board already making clear that it has no intention of bringing back the 63-year-old, who resigned earlier this month following the scandal.
It also followed fresh warnings from Trump's own Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, who said earlier on Sunday that the administration still wanted answers about Nvidia's sales of advanced computer chips to China .
Trump's latest intervention represents his strongest public endorsement yet of Huang's possible comeback , putting the president on a potential collision course with the company's leadership.
Last week, Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones delivered an unequivocal rejection of efforts to reinstate its former boss.
'The NVIDIA Board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,' Jones told investors during the company's quarterly earnings call.
President Donald Trump has launched a public campaign to reinstate Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO, insisting the billionaire's return would benefit both the technology giant and the country
Trump made his strongest appeal yet on Truth Social on Sunday night, personally urging Nvidia's board to rehire Huang despite its stated refusal to reinstate him
Huang was accused of carrying out an extramarital affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, of no relation, who was suspected of violating US sanctions on transporting AI chips into Beijing
When Huang resigned from Nvidia on November 12, the company appointed longtime chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO and launched a search for a permanent successor .
But despite a torrent of bad press aimed at Huang, including reports of allegedly abusive behavior to his staff and allegations of further extramarital affairs, Trump has refused to abandon his campaign to see Huang return to the top job.
At a White House news conference on Friday, the president passionately defended the technology pioneer, describing him as one of America's most valuable minds.
'We have to protect our brilliant people. Jensen is one of them,' Trump declared.
'I think the company if they were smart they'd take that brilliant man, accept an apology and let him go back to work.'
Trump also suggested Huang should make a public apology before returning to the company he co-founded in 1993.
His support comes amid mounting pressure from Silicon Valley figures, including Elon Musk, who have joined calls for Nvidia to reconsider the decision.
A campaign dubbed 'Stand With Jensen' has attracted widespread support from employees, investors and technology executives who believe the billionaire remains essential to the company's future.
Trump has repeatedly defended Huang following his resignation, describing him as one of America's brilliant minds and urging Nvidia's board to give him another chance
Longtime chief financial officer Colette Kress has been appointed as interim CEO while the company searches for a permanent successor
Reports emerged that one of the women the Nvidia CEO allegedly had an affair with, businesswoman Alice Huang, was suspected of being a Chinese spy
Investment firms Altimeter Capital Management and Atreides Management have also urged Nvidia's directors to keep their options open when deciding who should lead the semiconductor giant.
Huang himself has indicated he would welcome the opportunity to return.
In a social media statement last Tuesday, he acknowledged making 'serious mistakes' in his personal life and said he would be 'honored to answer these calls' if the board determined his reinstatement was in the company's best interests.
However, Nvidia's leadership appears determined to move forward without its longtime figurehead.
Jones has insisted the company acted in the interests of employees, customers and shareholders when it accepted Huang's resignation.
The board has also established a new committee dedicated to national security and export control oversight as federal authorities examine the company's dealings involving advanced artificial intelligence chips.
The scandal has placed Nvidia under intense scrutiny over its relationship with China, America's principal rival in the global race to dominate artificial intelligence.
Huang stepped down after admitting to extramarital relationships, including an affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, whose alleged intelligence connections are being examined by American authorities.
US investigators are also scrutinizing whether advanced Nvidia chips were improperly diverted to Chinese companies through businesses operating in Southeast Asia.
The allegations have not established that Jensen Huang knowingly participated in espionage or illegal chip transfers.
Nevertheless, the controversy has prompted congressional inquiries and questions about how Nvidia safeguarded sensitive technology while Huang was running the company.
CEO Jensen Huang's reign at AI tech giant Nvidia came to an abrupt end this month following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy
The Nvidia CEO and Alice Huang are seen posing at dinner together in a photo shared on social media (Source: Instagram)
Alice Huang is a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who became romantically involved with the married Nvidia founder
Huang, according to the complaint, acknowledged his infidelity to his wife of 41 years, Lori Huang, in an apology to employees after finally informing Nvidia's board about the relationship
Appearing on CBS's Face the Nation on Sunday, Bessent made clear that the administration was still demanding information from the chipmaker.
'We've been in touch with the temporary management, with the lead directors, with their lawyers, and we do need answers,' the Treasury secretary said.
'It behooves Nvidia to move quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was.'
Asked about Trump's support for Huang's reinstatement, Bessent stopped short of endorsing the president's position.
'I think we have to see where the buck stops,' he said.
The dispute comes at a critical moment for Nvidia, whose advanced processors underpin much of the world's rapidly expanding artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Despite the upheaval surrounding its founder, the company reported a staggering $116 billion in quarterly revenue last week, around double the figure from 2025.
Its financial strength has only intensified debate over whether Huang, widely credited with transforming Nvidia into a global technology powerhouse, should be allowed another chance.
For now, the company's board remains publicly opposed to his return.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | LIRR riders sharing phone location get $8 ticket warnings — despite claims of no tracking
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | LIRR riders sharing phone location get $8 ticket warnings — despite claims of no tracking
articles.content_orig:
They’re being tracked on the tracks!
Long Island Rail Road riders sharing their location are getting ticket activation warnings — despite officials’ claims that they wouldn’t monitor geodata to police commuters.
The LIRR hiked prices in January and started issuing a new $8 fine if riders didn’t activate their tickets on the TrainTime app prior to boarding, with the transit agency saying it would only use a “timekeeping function” to check if the rules were being broken.
But The Post found phones sharing their locations received warnings while phones not sharing didn’t receive any warnings — which cybersecurity experts said shows the app may be “abusing user data.”
“The tests [The Post ran] are pretty black and white — they’re clearly using some sort of location data when they say they’re not,” said Harry Maugans, a cybersecurity expert and privacy advocate.
“People should care about this, because if they don’t, one day we’re going to wake up in an Orwellian state,” said Maugans, who is CEO of data privacy firm Privacy Bee.
The Post used two phones with different location settings over multiple trips spanning various dates, with both phones having unactivated tickets at the start of a trip.
One phone, with its location set to “always” sharing, was consistently hit with pop-up late-activation warnings early in the ride that tell riders they’ll be surcharged for repeatedly violating the policy.
The other phone, with its location set to “never” sharing, was able to activate tickets without penalties or warnings — even after two or three stops into a trip after boarding.
The LIRR, which operates as one of the Metropolitan Transportation Authority’s commuter railroads, didn’t offer an explanation for the discrepancy.
The MTA only pointed to the TrainTime app’s terms of services when confronted with The Post’s findings.
The terms of service and conditions claim that location data is stored entirely separate from each customer’s TrainTime account.
The agency also didn’t respond to questions about what the stored data is used for.
LIRR tickets aren’t associated with a specific train, which experts said showed the app shouldn’t “know” if a user is on board a moving train except if the phone’s location is being used as a giveaway.
The TrainTime app’s vendor, Masabi, a London-based company whose ticketing software runs inside the app, said in its own privacy policy that it handles that rider data only as a processor, leaving the MTA in charge of how it’s used.
The Post has filed Freedom of Information Law requests regarding the TrainTime app and location data and is awaiting a response from the MTA.

articles.title_orig: GTA 6 New Update Releasing in Phases; Size Revealed
articles.title_zh: GTA 6 New Update Releasing in Phases; Size Revealed
articles.content_orig:
A dataminer has revealed that Rockstar will release a new GTA 6 update today in phases, and its size is 603 MB.
After 13 years, Rockstar has finally released a new installment in their acclaimed Grand Theft Auto franchise, and GTA 6 is living up to expectations. While it is a strong release, the game’s expansive nature means there are bound to be some issues that will need to be addressed post-launch. A new update might be coming soon to target those bugs.
A recent post from the reliable source PlayStation Game Size on X (formerly Twitter) informs players about the latest update for GTA 6. The update, version 01.002.002, will be released in phases worldwide. While it hasn’t been specified whether the rollout is regional, it appears that 33% of GTA 6 players can already download the new update. 66% of users will be able to access it in three hours, while the remaining 1% will receive the update in six hours.
GTA 6 – Update 01.002.002 33% of Users : Now Available. 66% of Users  : in 3h All Users : in 6h Update Size : 603 MB pic.twitter.com/bQ2frBuBfd
The update size has been revealed to be 603 MB, although it hasn’t been confirmed whether it’s the same for both platforms. Furthermore, Rockstar has not officially announced the update, so we don’t know what specific issues this new GTA 6 patch will address.
Since it has only been four days since the game’s release, it is speculated that the update will primarily focus on fixing bugs and glitches. However, we will have to wait for the official patch notes for this November 23 GTA 6 update to find out exactly what will be addressed.
What bugs and fixes do you want addressed in the latest GTA 6 update? Leave your thoughts down in the comments, and join the official Insider Gaming Discord server .
For more from Insider Gaming, read about GTA 3 having a $600,000 music budget that was never spent . Don’t forget to sign up for our weekly newsletter .

articles.title_orig: US Stock Futures Bounce After AI-Driven Correction: Markets Wrap
articles.title_zh: US Stock Futures Bounce After AI-Driven Correction: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
US stocks look set for a sharp bounce back Monday, following a punishing tech stock sell-off driven by fears about the durability of the AI investment boom.
Futures tied to the tech-focused Nasdaq-100 jumped 3.6% in premarket trading, while contracts tied to the S&P 500 and Dow gained 2.9% and 2%, respectively. Some of the biggest premarket gainers were technology stocks that have been pummelled recently, with Nvidia and the AI cloud infrastructure company CoreWeave each gaining more than 8%.
The rebound comes after a brutal downturn last week, during which all three major U.S. stock indexes recorded weekly losses of 8% or more. The S&P 500 ended the week with its seventh straight day of losses – its longest losing streak since February 2020. The Nasdaq, which plunged more than 5% Friday alone, is now sitting in the red for the year.
Monday’s rebound looks to be in large part “mechanical,” said Jonas Goltermann, chief markets economist at consultancy Capital Economics.
“It was just such a big sell-off (last week) and got a bit overdone,” he told CNN, calling Monday’s moves a “dead cat bounce” – trader speak for a brief recovery in stocks before a downward trend resumes.
“This is no longer a routine selloff,” Goltermann added, pointing to the fact that the benchmark S&P 500 is now down more than 10% from its recent high on October 6. “It’s very unusual to see a 10% drawdown so quickly from an all-time high… another substantial selloff is quite likely on that basis.”
Markets have been roiled by growing investor doubt about how sustainable the AI boom is. Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO last week did little to quell investor concerns about potential regulation, sky-high company valuations and a slowdown in AI investment, particularly for data centers.
Why Anthropic’s blockbuster debut didn’t ease Wall Street’s AI fears
“What began in October as a textbook rotation out of tech from extended levels has morphed into a broader risk-off move amid a succession of negative catalysts,” Deutsche Bank analysts wrote in a note Monday.
They cited the Democratic “blue wave” in the US midterms; the troubles at Nvidia, a company crucial to the AI rollout; the wave of equity hitting stock markets as firms tied to AI go public; “and a cluster of seemingly concurrent tech outages that have raised wider concerns.”
Markets in Asia were mixed Monday, with South Korea’s Kospi ending 3.3% lower, dragged down by declines in chip giants Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. Financial regulators in South Korea and China have announced measures recently to support markets.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, the world’s biggest chipmaker, climbed 1.5%, helping lift an index of Taiwan’s 50 largest companies by 2.25%.
In Europe, markets were largely positive in late morning trading. Dutch semiconductor-equipment maker ASML was up more than 5%.

articles.content_orig:
BEIJING, Nov 23 (Reuters) – China hopes Switzerland will ​oppose “Taiwan independence” ‌with concrete actions and “play a positive role in the ‌smooth ​resolution ⁠of China-EU ⁠economic and trade differences,” Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi ​told his Swiss counterpart ⁠on ⁠Monday.
The two countries ​should also conduct ​dialogue and cooperation ‌on artificial intelligence at bilateral and multilateral ⁠levels, Wang said, according to a summary ⁠of ‌their meeting ⁠released by ​the ‌Chinese foreign ministry.
The ​two also ⁠discussed Ukraine, the summary showed.

articles.title_orig: 'I was left broken' - Woman taking civil case against 'church that failed her'
articles.title_zh: 'I was left broken' - Woman taking civil case against 'church that failed her'
articles.content_orig:
Warning: This article contains details that some readers may find distressing.
A woman who is taking a civil case against her former church, over an allegation that she was groomed and sexually abused by a youth leader when she was a teen, has said she was failed by those who should have protected her.
Jessica, not her real name, had been a member of a youth group in a Church of Ireland parish in County Antrim when she said she was first sexually assaulted at the age of 17 by a much older, married man.
After she turned 18, she said she went on to become his "toy" and was coerced into months of what she described as non-consensual sex.
The Diocese of Connor, which oversees Jessica's former church, said it would be "inappropriate" to comment on the allegations given the matter was the subject of legal proceedings.
The alleged abuse happened about 20 years ago but a survivors' advocate warned that grooming continues to happen in faith settings, where young people are particularly vulnerable.
Nikella Holmes, who is a survivor of sexual abuse and who supports others with similar experiences, said more learning was needed in churches in order to protect young people from potential predators.
Jessica did not initially disclose her alleged abuse herself.
It was the youth leader who told the County Antrim church that the pair had been having a consensual affair.
Jessica said he had made the disclosure while he was under scrutiny for a separate unrelated issue, for which he was stood down from his youth leader role.
According to Jessica, the church wrongly accepted this at face value and did not view his disclosure as a safeguarding issue.
Years later, when she confronted a senior member of the church about how the matter was handled, she said they told her she had been viewed as someone who had been "groomed and taken advantage of".
Despite this, the church is defending Jessica's civil claim against it.
Jessica is now in her 30s and after years of therapy and support from her loved ones said she was finally "in a good place".
But the abuse she said she was subjected to had left her a "broken, young girl" and, at one point, feeling suicidal.
Jessica said that when the abuse began she had been having a hard time and that the youth leader offered her spiritual support and prayer.
She said he was someone in a "position of authority", whom she "looked up to and trusted and respected".
"I believe he saw my vulnerability. He was witness to what was going on in my life and how I was struggling to cope with various things," she said.
"It's only been in hindsight that I've realised that actually that behaviour from him was in fact grooming, and that was him manipulating me and getting alongside me for the wrong intentions."
She said: "He betrayed me spiritually, emotionally and physically."
When the initial alleged assault took place, Jessica said she had been at a gathering with the youth group, including people as young as 15.
"It was a crowded room full of people," she said.
"We were just watching TV at that point and the room was quite dark so no-one else was able to see. And he put his hand down my trousers and inside my underwear.
"I just froze. I went numb. I think I potentially stopped breathing for a few seconds. I was just in utter shock and couldn't feel my legs. My whole system literally shut down.
"From then on I basically became his toy and he had such a hold over me that I just felt so stuck. Anything he said went."
She said the sex that followed over the next number of months was not consensual.
"When the other party isn't actively engaging, I would deem that as not wanting to take part, especially given his position in the church and the age gap," she said.
"He just had utter control over me and my movements and my life. I would have been out for a run, his car would have pulled up alongside me: 'Get in.'"
Jessica said that as things progressed the youth leader told her he would kill himself if she told anyone.
She said that with the "weight of his life" on her she kept the secret in order to "somehow protect him".
According to Jessica, her alleged abuse was not viewed as a safeguarding issue when the youth leader disclosed what he described as their relationship to senior members of the church.
She said she was not asked at the time for her version of the events.
"The leadership received information from one side and I think the information they got from that side was the easier version for them to potentially digest," she said.
"It was never regarded as a safeguarding issue. They claimed that I was an adult, throughout it all, that I was over 18, and that all activities were consensual from both parties."
Shortly after the alleged abuse ended, Jessica said the church offered to pay for counselling and provided her with the name of a Christian counsellor.
About a decade later, after she had processed her "trauma", Jessica said she approached a senior member of the church and asked "some hard, honest questions" about what was done in the aftermath of the alleged abuse.
"The church had a duty of care to protect me, not only as one of their members but as a member of their youth, as a minor, essentially, when this all started," she said.
"And they didn't do that. And then later, as I went to them for help, they couldn't help me. They let me down."
Jessica later reported her allegations to the Police Service of Northern Ireland, which pursued a criminal investigation, but she said the Public Prosecution Service chose not to prosecute given the years that had passed.
The PPS told the BBC there was often a substantial period of time between the date of an alleged offence and the date of a person's first complaint, but that the "significant passage of time does not prevent the effective prosecution of sexual offences".
Jessica said she hoped that her civil case against her former church would help bring about change to the handling of safeguarding concerns.
That was something Nikella Holmes said she believed was needed.
Nikella was 15 when she was groomed and indecently assaulted two decades ago by a different youth leader at another church.
She said church could be "all-consuming" for young people and when they seek guidance and support from their seniors who hold positions of trust and authority, they are particularly vulnerable, even after they turn 18.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia Faces Fresh Questions Over China Chip Smuggling Probe
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Faces Fresh Questions Over China Chip Smuggling Probe
articles.content_orig:
Add Axios as your preferred source to
see more of our stories on Google.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at a May 2026 ceremony in China. Photo: Alex Wong/Getty Images
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday questioned whether Nvidia's earnings might have been inflated by inappropriate sales to China and urged the company to hire an outsider as CEO.
Why it matters: Nvidia is central to the AI economy, which has been key to U.S. economic growth.
Driving the news: In a Fox News appearance Sunday morning, Bessent said Nvidia owes the market an explanation amid allegations former CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a Chinese spy and oversaw sanctions-evading chip sales to Asian companies.
Bessent also said it was "obvious" that some companies doing business with Nvidia were shell companies for Chinese interests and accused the chipmaker of a "culture of noncompliance."
For the record: Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Bessent's remarks.
The intrigue: Huang has been a favorite of President Trump and other administration figures for some time, but Bessent has notably not been as effusive about him as others.
What to watch: Nvidia is due to report quarterly results on Tuesday, its first significant public comments since Huang resigned and CFO Collette Kress took over as acting CEO.

articles.title_orig: Seniors embrace Tesla automated driving technology despite questions about safety
articles.title_zh: Seniors embrace Tesla automated driving technology despite questions about safety
articles.content_orig:
Joan Spalding, 89, sits behind the wheel of her Tesla Model Y, equipped with Full-Self Driving (Supervised) technology, on a recent drive near her home in Evergreen, Colo. Jimena Peck for NPR hide caption
EVERGREEN, Colo. — Joan Spalding has driven the steep, winding road that leads to her house outside Denver for more than 50 years. But these days, the 89-year-old barely touches the steering wheel or the pedals.
Instead she tells the car where she wants to go, and presses a button on the large touch-screen in the dashboard of her Tesla Model Y.
"I just get in and go," Spalding says.
For all practical purposes, the car appears to be driving itself, navigating confidently on twisting roads through postcard valleys full of juniper and ponderosa pine.
"Now this is probably one of the narrowest roads," Spalding says, as the car pulls onto a dirt track that can barely fit two cars side by side, with a steep drop off to one side.
The Tesla handles the tight turns gracefully, even stopping to let an SUV squeeze by in the other lane.
Spalding was skeptical at first of what Tesla officially calls Full-Self Driving (Supervised), often abbreviated as FSD. It's a subscription service that drivers pay for, usually $99 dollars per month.
That was, until she saw what it could do.
"When I was driving," Spalding said, "I saw that the kind of things that it did were safer than what I would do."
Joan Spalding at her home in Evergreen, Colo. She was skeptical at first, but says she feels safer navigating the mountain roads with Tesla's driver-assistance technology. Jimena Peck for NPR hide caption
There are more older drivers on the road than ever, and families often struggle with the question of when it's time to stop driving. Now, seniors are using emerging technology to stay behind the wheel longer, specifically automated systems made by Tesla. But safety experts worry the company may be over-selling what its cars can do.
"It's not a technology that I would drive with. It's not a technology that I would suggest that my loved ones use. I think it has a few safety gaps that just make me uncomfortable," said Bryan Reimer, a research scientist at MIT, who studies how drivers interact with technology.
It's hard to know exactly how many seniors are using Tesla's automated driving system, but the numbers may be growing. Overall, Tesla says FSD has more than 1.7 million active subscriptions , an increase of 67% from a year ago. If the car-maker knows how many of those subscribers are seniors, it isn't saying.
Riding along with Joan Spalding, it's easy to understand the appeal for older drivers. The car gives her mobility and freedom that she wouldn't have otherwise.
Before she got her Tesla, Spalding had gotten into a number of minor fender benders. Then, two years ago, she was in a serious crash while she was trying to make a left turn.
"I made a wrong decision. I wasn't focusing on what I should be doing … I was lucky," she said. "But I realized then that my abilities were not where I wanted them to be."
Her son Mike Spalding had known for a while that his mother's driving was getting worse. He was already driving a Tesla, and it was his idea to get one for her.
Joan Spalding's son moves a mattress from the back of her Tesla Model Y. Spalding appreciates how her Tesla's rear seats fold, allowing her to sleep inside the vehicle while traveling. Jimena Peck for NPR hide caption
"It would be safer for mom if she was in a wreck because it's got all kinds of safety features. And then safer for people around her if we didn't have any more crashes. I've been driving one for years, and so I'd experimented with the Full Self-Driving and saw what it could do," Spalding said. "It's better than me."
Tesla agrees. The company claims that FSD is up to nine times safer than human driving. Tesla doesn't release much data about FSD, so it's impossible to independently verify whether its safety claims are true, Reimer said. He concedes Tesla's technology is impressive and is getting better all the time, but says it's not a replacement for a human driver — at least, not yet.
"Tesla has continually over-promised and under-delivered," Reimer said. "Full self-driving is not full self-driving, but yet the name feels so real."
If you read the fine print, FSD is not fully autonomous. The company always uses its full title — FSD (Supervised) — in official communications, to underscore the point. The driver is supposed to be paying attention at all times, in case the car encounters a situation FSD can't handle.
The problem, according to safety experts, is that human drivers tend to get complacent.
"It's good enough, often enough, where people go, 'The next time I'm in this similar situation, I know how it's going to behave,'" said Alexandra Mueller, a senior research scientist at the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, the nonprofit funded by the insurance industry.
But Mueller worries older drivers won't be ready or able to take control of the car in an emergency.
"This can be a huge problem," she said. "Ultimately it is very unsafe if you have drivers who are not fully competent due to age-related impairments or decline."
Tesla did not reply to requests for comment.
With her hands free, Joan Spalding prays with a rosary as she drives. Jimena Peck for NPR hide caption
The company has not said exactly how many senior drivers are using FSD to stay on the road longer, or even if that's something Tesla is tracking. But the company's CEO, Elon Musk, has encouraged the practice.
In a recent post on his social media platform X, Musk said that "Tesla self-driving gives mobility to seniors." Several times, he's amplified a video from a YouTube channel called TFLEV, featuring a 98-year-old man, who just bought his first Tesla.
"It has not made a mistake. And I've been driving it probably two or three months and it's not made an error in its driving, " the driver, Larry Dimmock, said in the video. "In fact, the other day it stopped. A chipmunk was crossing the road and there was no other traffic and it did not run over the chipmunk."
Musk reposted the video last month, saying, "At Tesla, we even care about the chipmunks." The clip has been viewed more than 3.5 million times.
"My moment of fame, I guess," Dimmock joked in an interview with NPR.
Dimmock says he's owned dozens of cars in his life, starting with a Ford Model A. He says he's still a pretty good driver at 98 — but not as good as his Tesla.
"I feel safer riding with this auto system than I do driving or riding with anybody. It's just been flawless," Dimmock said. "I'll get in the car and go somewhere, otherwise, I probably wouldn't."
Joan Spalding says self-driving technology allows her to live independently and remain in her cherished home. Jimena Peck for NPR hide caption
For Joan Spalding in Colorado, it's more than just a question of convenience. She says FSD is allowing her to live independently in the house that she and her late husband built more than 50 years ago.
"I love the solitude of being in that place and being by myself," she said.
Without the mobility that FSD gives her, Spalding said, she would likely have to find another place to live where she wouldn't need to drive.
"I'd have to move," she said. "This way, I think I can drive it for as long as I want to. I don't see any reason why not."

articles.title_orig: Drone attacks kill four near Sudan’s capital, damage UN building
articles.title_zh: Drone attacks kill four near Sudan’s capital, damage UN building
articles.content_orig:
Drone attacks blamed on Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have killed four people in and around the capital, Khartoum, and damaged a United Nations building, according to local reports and UN officials.
The attacks early on Sunday struck residential areas as Sudanese air defences responded to drones reportedly targeting government buildings and Khartoum’s airport.
The strikes have raised fresh concerns about the growing danger to civilians and aid workers as Sudan ‘s war increasingly relies on drones.
Explosions were heard across the capital between approximately 2am (00:00 GMT) and 4:30am (02:30 GMT), according to witnesses cited by the AFP news agency, as the army attempted to intercept the drones.
Al Jazeera’s AlMigdad Alruhaid reported from the city of Omdurman, across the Nile from Khartoum, that three people were killed and nine wounded when a drone struck a home in northern Omdurman.
A child was also killed in a separate attack south of the capital.
In the village of Jebel Aulia, about 45km (28 miles) south of Khartoum, a witness told AFP that a drone hit the home of a mosque official who calls worshippers to prayer. Residents searched the wreckage for trapped relatives.
The UN’s humanitarian coordinator in Sudan, Denise Brown, said on Sunday that one of its buildings had been damaged while staff were inside.
The UN’s humanitarian office, which coordinates emergency relief, condemned the danger to its personnel in a civilian neighbourhood, calling it “unacceptable”.
A Sudanese army source told AFP on Sunday that the drones had been launched from neighbouring Ethiopia’s Bahir Dar airport. The allegation could not be independently verified.
Ethiopia has previously denied Sudanese accusations that it allows the RSF to carry out attacks from its territory.
Sudan has also lodged complaints with the UN Security Council, the body responsible for international peace and security, and the African Union, a continental organisation, over alleged drone operations originating in Ethiopia.
Separately on Sunday, Sudan’s government accused RSF fighters of executing captured soldiers in southeastern Blue Nile state, near the Ethiopian border.
The government condemned the alleged killings as violations of international humanitarian law. The accusation has not been independently verified.
Both the RSF and the Sudanese army are relying more frequently on drones to hit enemy targets. More than 1,100 were killed by drones in the first half of this year, according to the United Nations.
The UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) has said that drone attacks account for about two-thirds of children killed or injured in Sudan from the period of January to September.
The war in Sudan between the army and the RSF began in April 2023. It has led to one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, with 13 million people displaced and some regions facing famine.

articles.title_orig: Billionaire Bill Ackman Sounds the Alarm on Wall Street's Next Big Risk
articles.title_zh: Billionaire Bill Ackman Sounds the Alarm on Wall Street's Next Big Risk
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Billionaire investor Bill Ackman thinks the Federal Reserve is about to make a big mistake.
In his view, the central bank is trying too hard to fix its long-running mistake on inflation.
"I think the Fed is about to make another mistake on December 9th. Financial conditions have tightened massively. For example, SpaceX ( SPCX ), an investment-grade company, just raised secured debt financing at an 8.259% interest rate versus below 6% for its unsecured bond offering at the time of its IPO. The cost of equity capital has also increased materially with the recent substantial decline in the stock market," the CEO of Pershing Square said in a new X post .
He added, "The Fed's 2% inflation ambition is misguided. Geopolitical risk, the required investment in global military spending, deglobalization and tariffs, and massive AI infrastructure and related energy investment are features of the world that did not exist when the 2% target was set. 3% inflation is a more realistic ambition in the new world. The Fed will put the U.S. and the world in recession if it continues to raise rates in a failed attempt to drive inflation to 2%."
Of course, Ackman is talking his book. Lower interest rates would benefit the stock market and his many stock holdings, such as Microsoft and Netflix.
Moreover, it's hard to argue that inflation hasn't worsened, or that need to act more aggressively to bring it under contr' it under control.
The inflation picture has deteriorated in recent months, with the October Consumer Price Index (CPI) showing prices rising 0.4% month over month, following a 0.6% increase in September. Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, rose another 0.3%, marking the third consecutive month at that pace and suggesting underlying price pressures remain stubborn.
The Federal Reserve's preferred measure of inflation, the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, was up 3.6% year over year in September. Core PCE clocked in at 3.1% — both well above the Fed's 2% target.
Inflation doesn't appear to be cooling fast enough, raising the possibility that interest rates may need to stay higher for longer or even move higher again.
The Fed lifted interest rates in September after sticky inflation readings , fueled in part by the AI boom and rising energy costs , forced central bankers back into tightening mode. The rate hike marked the central bank's first increase since July 2023.
At its late-October meeting, the Fed held steady, which many now see as a mistake.
"If you break out the categories of where the inflation is, it's kind of in the wrong, more disturbingly persistent categories like services, healthcare, a series of things that really can't be coming from tariffs or oil prices," Chicago Federal Reserve president Austan Goolsbee said at Yahoo Finance's Invest earlier this month . "I think it's worth being sober-minded at a moment like this that we're inching our way into a territory that's historically a tough spot for any central bank to try to get rid of that inflation. We'd do well to try to prevent it from getting worse."
Brian Sozzi is Yahoo Finance's Executive Editor, host of the Sozzi Unleashed morning show, the ' Power Players With Brian Sozzi' podcast and a member of Yahoo Finance's editorial leadership team.

articles.title_orig: North Korea’s Kim Jong Un Welcomes New Envoys ‘Friendly Toward Us’
articles.title_zh: North Korea’s Kim Jong Un Welcomes New Envoys ‘Friendly Toward Us’
articles.content_orig:
This picture taken on November 22, 2026 and released from North Korea's official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) on November 23, 2026, shows North Korean leader Kim Jong Un (R) delivering a speech at a ceremony for the presentation of credentials by foreign ambassadors at the headquarters building of the Party Central Committee in Pyongyang on November 23, 2026. (KCNA via KNS / AFP Photo)
Kim Jong Un said North Korea would strive to achieve “power and capability” to ensure its security and peace but would not pursue supremacy, state media reported on Nov. 23.
Kim made the remarks at a ceremony to receive credentials from newly appointed ambassadors, including Russia’s, in a rare departure from protocol, as the task has traditionally been performed by a senior official rather than Kim himself.
The ceremony followed Kim’s snubbing of U.S. President Donald Trump’s overtures last week during Trump’s visit to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.
Trump left Asia late Nov. 19 after a landmark trilateral summit with the Chinese and Russian presidents, without meeting Kim, as Trump had suggested he might.
“The world is now witnessing an unstable security crisis and political and economic chaos round the globe,” Kim said at the event, according to the official Korean Central News Agency, without elaborating.
“The present international situation is bringing about a significant change in our understanding of national sovereignty and security,” he said.
Pyongyang’s diplomatic goal is to “expand and develop foreign relations under the ideals of independence, peace and friendship on the principle of defending the national sovereignty and security,” he added.
“The DPRK neither pursues supremacy nor expansion,” he said, using the initials of the North’s official name.
Armenia unveiled a draft of a new constitution on Nov. 23, removing references on territorial claims against Türkiye and Azerbaijan in a major step toward signing a formal peace agreement with Baku.
Ford Europe President Jim Baumbick criticized the exclusion of vehicles made in Türkiye under the EU’s proposed “Made in Europe” rules, saying the move would penalize Ford for investments it made under the rules in place at the time.
European football officials highlighted Turkish clubs’ commercial potential and the need for financial sustainability at a summit in Istanbul on Nov. 17.

articles.title_orig: Artificial superintelligence ‘arriving’, warns top Meta executive
articles.title_zh: Artificial superintelligence ‘arriving’, warns top Meta executive
articles.content_orig:
Meta’s top AI executive has sounded the alarm about the risk of humanity losing control of AI, warning that superintelligence that far exceeds the human intellect is imminent.
Meta Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang issued the warning on Sunday after an employee at AI giant Anthropic announced that he had used Claude to solve the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most difficult problems in mathematics.
Wang said the breakthrough dwarfed any human achievement for “sheer intellectual might”.
The 29-year-old executive said the milestone showed that emerging AI models will be “clearly superhuman” at improving themselves, as well as “massively accelerating” research in fields such as biology, armaments and economics.
“Superintelligence is arriving,” Wang said on X.
“How humanity acts over the next year will have great consequence on what future world we live in.”
Wang, who co-founded Scale AI before joining Meta as the tech giant’s first chief AI officer last year, said it is unlikely humankind will be able to control AI that achieves unconstrained recursive self-improvement or is “1000x smarter and more capable than humans in every field.”
“Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully,” Wang said.
AI safety advocates have identified recursive self-improvement – where AI models become capable of advancing without human input – as a critical tipping point after which humanity could lose the ability to control the technology.
While the risks of frontier AI have stoked intense debate in Silicon Valley, there is no consensus on how to maximise the benefits of the technology without exposing humanity to catastrophic risks.
Meta has largely positioned itself on the more optimistic side of the debate, with CEO and cofounder Mark Zuckerberg rejecting calls by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman for a coordinated slowdown in development to beef up guardrails.
In an essay published in August, Zuckerberg lamented that discussions about AI were “filled with doom” and said the technology should lead to “more people sharing greater prosperity, health and freedom.”
In his post on Sunday, Wang criticised “lazy thinking” within the AI industry that he said treated superintelligence as inevitable.
“We should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI. We should endeavour ourselves to build a technology which delivers a positive future for humanity, where all humans have greater agency and empowerment,” Wang said.
“I strongly believe this is possible, but likely involves the whole industry taking meaningfully different actions from the “default path” in front of us.”

articles.title_orig: China’s Growing Ambitions in Very Low Earth Orbit
articles.title_zh: China’s Growing Ambitions in Very Low Earth Orbit
articles.content_orig:
Join War on the Rocks and gain access to content trusted by policymakers, military leaders, and strategic thinkers worldwide.
A new front in the U.S.-Chinese space race is emerging in the lowest reaches of space : very low Earth orbit, the untapped orbital regime below 320 kilometers. There, China is laying the groundwork for a significant presence, with announced plans for more than 2,200 satellites and an aggressive deployment timeline through 2030.
Chinese satellites at these lower altitudes would allow the People’s Liberation Army to conduct more frequent and detailed surveillance of U.S. forces, and improve Chinese military survivability in conflict. Very low Earth orbit’s denser atmosphere helps protect satellites from debris and nuclear radiation that could disable spacecraft in higher orbits, making China’s space architecture more resilient.
These are strategic advantages the United States should be prepared to counter. The answer is not to match China satellite for satellite, but to improve American space capabilities and survivability. Washington should respond by expanding orbital diversity across its space architecture, assessing where very low Earth orbit offers operational advantages worth pursuing, and working with industry to coordinate the orbit’s development.
As executives at Albedo, a U.S. startup building satellites for very low Earth orbit , we have a stake in the future of this orbital regime. We recognize that the orbit’s advantages come with trade-offs, which we discuss openly below. But our roles have given us a close-up view of its evolution from an experimental frontier into a domain of strategic competition, and we believe China’s ambitions there warrant far more attention in Washington.
Sign Up for Our Newsletter
Satellites operate at vastly different altitudes depending on their missions. At roughly 36,000 kilometers, geostationary Earth orbit keeps satellites over the same region for persistent communications and surveillance. Medium Earth orbit, between roughly 2,000 and 36,000 kilometers, hosts GPS and other navigation satellites. Most new satellite activity is in low Earth orbit , extending to roughly 2,000 kilometers, with most satellites above 450 kilometers. Cheaper to reach than higher orbits, low Earth orbit offers advantages for communications and remote sensing, but is increasingly crowded with satellites and debris. That crowding and the advantages of proximity have drawn both government and commercial interest to very low Earth orbit.
Very low Earth orbit refers to the orbital regime of 320 kilometers and below, where the atmosphere starts to become dense enough to both rapidly clear debris and shield satellites from radiation, benefits that grow stronger as altitude decreases. Since these altitudes lie within the upper atmosphere, drag and atomic oxygen have historically made sustained operations difficult. Though advances in propulsion technology, surface materials, and spacecraft design are now overcoming these challenges, operating so close to Earth still comes with trade-offs. Satellites must expend power thrusting against drag, and while purpose-built designs can support lifespans of around five years , those lifespans can vary as solar activity changes atmospheric density . Another trade-off is coverage: each satellite sees less of Earth , requiring more satellites for broader coverage.
Where proximity to Earth matters, however, very low Earth orbit can bring significant benefits . Remote sensing satellites can achieve substantially higher resolution, helping operators more precisely track military forces on Earth. Proximity also brings stronger communications signals and lower latency, useful for tactical missions at the edge.
Very low Earth orbit also offers distinct resiliency and sustainability advantages. Because the atmosphere is roughly 100 times denser than in higher low Earth orbit, debris that would remain in low Earth orbit for years clears from very low Earth orbit in days to weeks , reducing collision risks for satellites. That same atmosphere provides natural shielding against persistent radiation effects of an orbital nuclear detonation , should one occur during a conflict. This would allow satellites to remain operational even if radiation disrupts those in higher orbits.
The orbit’s economics differ, too. Drag can raise operating and replenishment costs. But smaller, cheaper payloads can match or exceed the performance of larger ones higher up. And for missions requiring protection against nuclear effects, the orbit’s natural shielding avoids hardening costs that would be prohibitively expensive for constellations in higher orbits .
It is these benefits that have made very low Earth orbit a growing priority within China’s space plans. Since 2022, China has successfully operated at least a half-dozen demonstration missions in very low Earth orbit , proving its ability to sustain satellites there. China is now building on those demonstrations with plans to deploy very low Earth orbit constellations at a scale unmatched by any other government.
Publicly announced Chinese plans project more than 2,200 very low Earth orbit satellites, spanning remote sensing, communications, and computing missions. With only about a dozen total satellites operating at these altitudes today, such a buildout would transform very low Earth orbit into a proliferated layer of China’s space infrastructure. The timeline is uncertain, but the trajectory is clear. One senior member of the Chinese Academy of Engineering — the nation’s top engineering academy — recently called the next five years a “critical window” for China in very low Earth orbit , and that the country “must complete the transition from technology experimentation to large-scale application.”
China’s clearest attempt to turn very low Earth orbit into a surveillance layer is the China Aerospace Science and Industry Corporation’s Chutian constellation. Announced in 2023, Chutian’s bullet-shaped satellites house many types of remote sensing payloads , with onboard data processing and intersatellite links to coordinate as one network. After at least three successful demonstrations, the company aims for 300 satellites by 2030 and potentially more than 500 thereafter. The constellation is designed to observe any point on Earth as frequently as every 15 minutes — a rate which would allow the People’s Liberation Army to compress its sensor-to-shooter timeline.
The most ambitious plan comes from Hangsheng Satellite, a commercial satellite manufacturer. In August 2026, Hangsheng announced plans to build a 1,920-satellite very low Earth orbit communications and computing constellation . Its plan calls for two demonstrations in 2027, then 24 validation satellites before scaling deployment through 2030 — a demanding manufacturing and launch schedule. But once deployed, the constellation would combine stronger radiofrequency links with very low Earth orbit’s resilience to debris and persistent nuclear radiation, creating a more survivable communications and computing layer. In a conflict that disrupted low Earth orbit, such an architecture could give the Chinese military another layer through which to process, fuse, and distribute information.
Chinese startups are also pursuing very low Earth orbit. In December 2024, AIRSAT, a spin-out of the state-run Aerospace Information Research Institute, launched Haishao-1, China’s first very low Earth orbit synthetic aperture radar satellite . Operating as low as 300 kilometers, its orbit concentrates coverage on the South China Sea and Taiwan, enabling up to 5.7 times more daily observations of the region than current Chinese synthetic aperture radar satellites. Another startup, C-Space, is developing a 48-satellite imagery constellation , alongside communications and navigation capabilities .
China is also coordinating its ambitions through a very low Earth orbit industry alliance chaired by the Chinese Academy of Sci

articles.title_orig: Ukraine blows up Russian warship in Libya’s Benghazi naval base
articles.title_zh: Ukraine blows up Russian warship in Libya’s Benghazi naval base
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine sank a Russian warship docked in Libya and disabled a cargo vessel off the North African country’s coast, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Monday, in Kyiv’s latest attack on Russian assets far from the frontlines.
The warship — identified as the 344-foot navy corvette Merkury — was attacked with seven maritime drones, sinking the ship and destroying a combat helicopter on board, Zelensky said in a post to Telegram.
Dramatic footage Zelensky released showed Ukrainian sea drones speeding towards the ship –– one of the newest ships in Russia’s fleet — which erupted into a giant ball of flames in the dock in Benghazi in eastern Libya. Photos taken by satellite imagery company Vantor showed the vessel submerged following the attack.
Ukraine’s second target was cargo ship the MV ANGARA which Zelensky said was being used by Russia to transport weapons.
The drone boats were “transported to the designated location and launched from a so-called ‘mothership,’” said Ukraine’s intelligence agency.
Russia said it had “taken note” of Zelensky’s statement about the attacks, which came hours after a suspected Ukrainian drone hit a Russian cargo ship about 2,000 miles away in the Baltic Sea.
“Our defense ministry is handling this,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Monday. “Likewise, any information – should it be deemed necessary to release any – will be provided through the defense ministry.”
The Ukrainian strikes also came days after a historic summit between US President Donald Trump, Russian leader Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping failed to make any progress towards ending Moscow’s war in Ukraine.
The 1,800 ton Merkury was in Benghazi to refuel under a maritime cooperation agreement before it intended to return to Russia, according to Libya’s Government of National Stability (GNS).
It incorporates some of Moscow’s latest shipbuilding technology, including radio absorption materials and a hull and superstructure designed to decrease its radar signature, Russian state media TASS reported when the ship joined the fleet in May 2023.
The GNS, which controls eastern Libya, said it has launched a joint investigation with Russia into the incident. It said it was not a party to the Russia-Ukraine war, and would not allow its territory to be turned into an “arena for settling scores.”
CNN has previously reported on Ukraine’s presence in Libya, Mali, Chad, Niger, Sudan and Burkina Faso as it tries to counter Russia’s growing influence in Africa, particularly the mineral-rich, coup-prone Sahel region.
Oil-rich and war-torn Libya is ruled by two governments: the UN-backed Government of National Unity (GNU) in the west, based in Tripoli, and the GNS in the east.
One Ukrainian naval drone operator deployed in Libya told CNN earlier this year his unit was using a military base in Misrata, a city east of Tripoli, as a launchpad to attack Russia’s shadow fleet in the Mediterranean in exchange for training local forces.
Asked about the weekend attacks on Monday, the operator told CNN: “We are doing what we can. And we can (do) a lot.”
As the Merkury erupted in flames Sunday, a cross-border firefighting operation was underway roughly 2,000 miles away in the Baltic Sea, where one day earlier a Russian cargo ship was struck by suspected Ukrainian drones, according to the Finnish military.
Emergency services from Finland, Russia and Estonia were working to put out a blaze on the Sparta II, in a rare instance of cooperation between Russia and the NATO members and steadfast Ukrainian allies.
Ukraine is fighting Russia anywhere it can – even in the deserts of Africa
The Merkury joins some 40 other Russian naval vessels lost in the war, most notable among those the guided-missile cruiser Moskva, the flagship of Moscow’s Black Sea fleet, sunk by a Ukrainian missile attack in April 2022.
Naval analyst Carl Schuster told CNN protecting ships in foreign ports is difficult for any navy.
“When a warship is in a foreign port, the host country is responsible for the ship’s physical security and protection,” he said.
A foreign vessel must be absolutely certain it is under attack before it can engage an enemy in port, and Libyan security is circumspect, Schuster said.
Ukraine has a large merchant fleet that can “provide a lot of seemingly innocent launch platforms” for attacks like the one in Benghazi, he added.
“We are looking at a new era of maritime unconventional warfare,” Schuster said.
This story has been updated with additional details.
CNN’s Kosta Gak, Farida Elsebai, Ivana Kottasová, Max Saltman and Anna Chernova contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: China reiterates stance on US export controls after Trump’s chip remarks
articles.title_zh: China reiterates stance on US export controls after Trump’s chip remarks
articles.content_orig:
Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney shakes hands with China's President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit on Nov. 19, 2026.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is placing particular focus on renewing relations with China as he aims to deepen international trade ties and diversify from U.S. reliance amid a three-month-long trade war with the U.S.
When asked what cards Canada holds in its ongoing talks with Washington, Carney, who recently announced a new partnership with the E.U. , pointed to the country's budding relationships elsewhere.
“Our cards are that everyone else in the world wants to deal with us,” he said Wednesday during a remote interview with the New York Times from Shenzhen, China, where he was among the world leaders attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit . "If the U.S. doesn't want to do the deal, we're busy.” His remarks came in the wake of President Donald Trump's claim that the U.S. holds “all the cards” after trade talks collapsed in August, leading to both sides enforcing heavy retaliatory tariffs .
Carney and Trump had a meeting on the sidelines of APEC, but aside from a commitment to “continue” negotiations and stay in close contact, no progress was made. However, Carney painted his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in a much more positive light. Ahead of the summit, Carney and Xi announced a Canada-China trade pact , which provided additional tariff relief on Canadian food and agricultural exports into China, and in return saw Canada agree to extend tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by two years.
Carney, who is promoting a “Canada Strong” platform as he aims to build economic resilience at home, touted the expansion of the trade arrangement with China as something that will deliver “greater certainty and prosperity for all Canadians.” He also praised the negotiation process with China, saying: “They’re very professional. They move forward in a very linear fashion.”
In an eight-day tour that took him from a European summit in Ireland to the Philippines, Cambodia, and finally China for the APEC gathering, Carney forged ahead with his plan to diversify Canada's economy away from its dependence on the U.S., which by far remains the country's largest trading partner .
Experts say Canada's progress in deepening its economic relationships with China could challenge Trump's insistence that Washington holds the upper hand in trade negotiations.
“Part of the Trump Administration’s [belief] is that everybody needs the U.S. more than anything else, and therefore the U.S. has maximum leverage,” says Jennifer Hillman, co-director of the Institute of International Economic Law at Georgetown University. “What this is clearly saying is that Canada can afford to be less willing to give the U.S. whatever it asks for [in negotiations], because they have other options.”
China has the world's second-largest economy , behind only the U.S., giving it the potential to become a much larger market for Canadian goods than some of the other countries Carney has sought to deepen relations with.
“China represents a very big market and the potential of a really big trading partner,” says Lori Turnbull, a professor in the Faculty of Management at Dalhousie University, noting it could be a leverage point in U.S. negotiations. “Doing a deal with a country like China is something that [the U.S.] will care about because of the size of China's economy and its competitive relationship with the U.S.”
Carney's latest push to strengthen trade ties with Beijing forms part of a months-long effort to renew Canada-China relations. In January, he met with Xi to forge what he called a “ new strategic partnership ,” agreeing to allow in up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles at a tariff of 6.1%, rather than the previous 100% levy. China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola seeds, a major Canadian export.
The move drew criticism from Trump, who said that “China will eat Canada alive, completely devour it, including the destruction of their businesses, social fabric, and general way of life.”
While Canada's closer relationship with China could strengthen its hand in negotiations, experts also warn that it could backfire.
Turnbull points to the latest agreement to extend tariff exemptions on Chinese steel and aluminum as a potential source of tension with Washington. “Things like reducing tariffs on select steel and aluminum products coming from China is something that might make the U.S. and not just Donald Trump, but also [U.S. Trade Representative] Jamieson Greer angry,” she suggests.
Steel, aluminum, and auto tariffs were among the major points of contention when U.S.-Canada trade negotiations broke down in August, with both sides accusing each other of walking back commitments.
Carney, however, has played down concerns that Canada's growing trade relationship with China is a major issue for Trump.
“In my conversation with the President, he’s tried to understand where we are with China, where we’re going with China,” said Carney during a news conference in Shenzhen. “I shouldn’t speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it’s not the top issue at all.”
Meanwhile, some Canadian officials have voiced concerns on expanding trade with China.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford warned Carney on Monday against opening the door for more Chinese-made EV vehicles in Canada, arguing the “government’s focus needs to be on protecting Canadian auto workers, not undermining them by importing even more state-subsidized cheap Chinese cars.”
Michael Chong, a lawmaker from Canada’s Conservative Party, during a press conference on Wednesday supported maintaining a dialogue with Beijing, but described Carney’s budding strategic partnership with China as a “risky gambit,” citing potential “national security” concerns.
In 2025, Ottawa identified China as one of the main perpetrators of foreign interference and espionage against Canada alongside other countries such as Russia and Iran. The Canadian government’s own analysis of Canada-China relations also points out that there are "associated risks” in broader trade cooperation in key areas, such as “prevalent and persistent intellectual property theft, and the risk of diversion of sensitive goods and technologies intended for civilian use for military purposes and applications.”
Carney said ahead of his Asia trip that he would raise concerns about foreign interference in his meeting with Xi. "The advantage of these meetings is you can raise issues directly and frankly,” he told reporters in Montreal on Nov. 10. Carney added that he would stress the importance Canada places on "the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries.”
In a press briefing during the APEC summit, Carney emphasized that Canada's trade with China is largely focused on commodities, rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors.
“We are exporting canola, we are exporting pork. We are exporting halibut,” Carney said , also citing liquefied natural gas and oil. “These are important industries. These are not cutting-edge semi-conductors.”
Experts point out that Canada could pursue deeper cooperation with other international partners in sectors where a closer relationship with China would be more difficult, including defense and advanced technology.
“[Canada] is not going to partner with China on defense, security, AI, and digital technology, things like that would be very difficult. [Carney] would have an impossible time trying to convince Canadians that's what we should be doing,” says Turnbull. “For those things, [Canada] would be putting [its] arms around the European Union.”
In September, the European Union unveiled its vision for Canada to become an “associate member” of the bloc. During an E.U.-Canada summit in Montreal in October, the two sides underscored their commitment to this plan, paving the way for deeper cooperation in areas including A

articles.title_orig: Russian ships hit by Ukrainian drones off Libya coast, Zelensky says
articles.title_zh: Russian ships hit by Ukrainian drones off Libya coast, Zelensky says
articles.content_orig:
A Russian warship was sunk by Ukrainian drones at a port in Libya on Sunday, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
On Sunday morning, the government that controls eastern Libya said there had been an explosion on the warship at the Benghazi naval base, while it was docking for fuel and supplies ahead of its return to Russia.
Zelensky said the attack hit a second Russian vessel, a cargo ship which he claimed was being used to transport weapons.
The health ministry said it had received injured people from a commercial ship that was targeted off the coast of the port. It is not clear whether this is the same vessel as the one Ukraine has claimed responsibility for.
Moscow has not yet commented on the attack.
In a statement on Monday, Zelensky praised an "exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia's war".
Seven naval drones were deployed to target and sink the corvette Merkury, one of Russia's newest ships, Zelensky wrote. He added that a Ka-27 combat helicopter was also destroyed.
The Ukrainian president said the second ship was the MV ANGARA, a Russian container carrier.
The attack came the day after a Russian cargo vessel was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland . The Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning.
Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has not commented.
The UN mission in Libya expressed "serious concern" over the attacks on Sunday, calling for "an immediate, independent and transparent investigation".
"Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts," the UNSMIL wrote on X.
Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship that was struck in the morning engulfed in flames and smoke. Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC also shows a boat on fire at 05:47 GMT at the Benghazi port.
US-based intelligence firm Vantor collected high-resolution images that it said showed Project 20380 Steregushchiy-class corvette (Merkury) - a Russian navy ship - moored in the port on Saturday, and on Sunday showed most of the same ship capsized and sunk with only the forward bow still visible.
The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship - which it did not name or identify - was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.
Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.
GNS condemned the attack on a ship inside a Libyan port, and called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty. It said Libya was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.
Separately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.
GNU said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".
Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.
Benghazi is more than 2,000 km (1,243 miles) away from the Russian capital Moscow.
In March, Russia accused Ukraine of targeting the Russian tanker Arctic Metagaz in the Mediterranean between Libya and Malta with "uncrewed sea drones" launched from the Libyan coast.
As well as having an economic impact on Russia, hampering the ability of their so-called shadow fleet of tankers to export oil and gas, attacks like this are seen as humiliating to the Kremlin, according to Harchaoui.
But it is not only Moscow that will want to react to this latest incident. The ship was in the region as part of a deal with the government of eastern Libya - allied with Khalifa Haftar, commander of the Libyan National Army.
Harchaoui said Haftar will take the attack as a personal slight. "You're going to have a response by the Haftar family. They will ask questions about who is hosting the Ukrainians."
Additional reporting by Benedict Garman and Shayan Sardarizadeh, BBC Verify
