articles.title_orig: Turkey: Thousands protest closure of critical media outlets
articles.title_zh: Turkey: Thousands protest closure of critical media outlets
articles.content_orig:
Several thousand people in Istanbul took to the streets on Sunday to protest the closure of several opposition-linked media outlets in Turkey .
Protesters chanted, cheered, and whistled as they marched several kilometers through the city, calling for press freedom and freedom of expression.
They carried a huge banner that read: "We want freedom of thought, freedom of the press, and freedom for journalists." The protesters were also carrying placards that read, "The press cannot be silenced."
Turkey's main opposition party, Yeni Parti, called for a protest just days after police raided Sozcu TV , one of the last opposition-aligned television channels.
Senior staff members were arrested during the raid. A government-appointed trustee was installed, and the TV company was placed under compulsory administration.
It was the third takeover in a year following similar actions against Tele1, Halk TV, Turkey's most-watched news channel , and the leading digital news website, T24.
Timur Soykan, a journalist who was briefly detained for criticizing the government, said that the government was doing everything in its power to silence journalists but was failing to do so.
Soykan asked the public to support Halk TV journalists, who plan to continue broadcasting on a new YouTube channel.
Over the past decade, press freedom has faced sustained pressure in the form of prosecutions, digital censorship, and government accusations that journalists are spreading "fake news."
In the last two months alone, Turkey has arrested several journalists for their reporting on a multibillion-dollar investment fund scandal. At least two of the journalists remain in pretrial detention.
According to the media rights group MLSA, twenty-five journalists are currently imprisoned in Turkey.
This year, Reporters Without Borders ranked Turkey 163rd out of 180 countries in its Press Freedom Index.

articles.title_orig: NVIDIA’s emergency SSD write fix may need another fix
articles.title_zh: NVIDIA’s emergency SSD write fix may need another fix
articles.content_orig:
NVIDIA released driver 621.35 to address excessive SSD writes.
NVIDIA released GeForce Hotfix Driver 621.35 on November 20 to address excessive SSD writes caused by recent GPU drivers. However, users are now reporting that the update does not completely resolve the problem. Background writes can return after several hours of system uptime, even when the PC is idle.
The issue was originally reported with GeForce drivers 621.14 and 621.24. The NVIDIA Display Container process was repeatedly writing data to the nvlog.nvlgstg log file. Some users recorded up to 30 GB of unnecessary writes per hour. NVIDIA acknowledged the issue under bug ID 7116722 and released 621.35 specifically to address it.
One of the users tested three driver versions on a system equipped with an RTX 4090 and a Samsung 990 PRO 2TB SSD. The hotfix initially appeared to work, with the NVIDIA process recording just 90.8 KB of additional I/O writes during the first hour. However, after nine hours of overnight idle time, the same process accumulated another 40.85 GB of writes, averaging approximately 4.54 GB per hour.
Comment by u/Nestledrink from discussion in nvidia
The user also checked HWiNFO64 and the SSD’s S.M.A.R.T. statistics. These showed 36 GB of additional SSD host writes during the same period, confirming actual storage activity rather than relying only on process I/O counters. The previous 621.24 driver produced higher write rates in this user’s tests, while rolling back to 621.01 reduced NVIDIA’s background activity to a few megabytes.
Other Redditors have reported similar results, although some users say the hotfix works correctly on their systems. This suggests that the problem may depend on specific configurations or conditions that have yet to be established.
Interestingly, NVIDIA representative Manuel@NVIDIA confirmed on the company’s official forums that the issue does not affect GeForce RTX 50 series graphics card s. However, some owners are reporting otherwise. One RTX 5090 user recorded approximately 47 GB of writes from an NVIDIA process, while another RTX 5080 owner reported 57 GB in a single day. These reports do not establish whether the same driver bug affects RTX 50 series GPUs, but they appear to contradict NVIDIA’s statement.
Some say it resolved the issue, while others continue to experience excessive writes after extended uptime. Users experiencing the problem can check NVIDIA-related disk activity through Windows Resource Monitor. Rolling back to 621.01 has worked for several affected users.

articles.title_zh: Zelenskyy says Ukraine behind drone attacks on Russian ships near Libya
articles.content_orig:
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Ukrainian forces sank ⁠a Russian warship off the coast of Libya, hailing an “exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia’s war”.
Zelenskyy said in a statement on Monday that Ukrainian forces also hit a Russian dry ⁠cargo ship, which he said Russia used to transport weapons.
Zelenskyy said the Merkury, one of Russia’s newest warships, sank after Ukrainian forces launched seven naval drones on Sunday. A KA-27 combat helicopter was also destroyed in the attack, he said.
He confirmed that Ukraine’s forces also attacked the MV Angara, a cargo ship . Libya’s eastern health ministry said that all crew members had been rescued and were receiving treatment.
Authorities in eastern Libya said in a statement that the ship was docked in the port when the explosion occurred.
“The ship was en route back to Russia and its stop was for refuelling and resupply. It is suspected that the ship was attacked by drones”.
The United Nations has called for an independent investigation into Sunday’s drone attacks .
On Monday, the United Nations Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”.
“Libya cannot afford and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts,” UNSMIL wrote on X.
The eastern administration did not identify who was behind Sunday’s attack but said Libya was “not a party to the Russian-Ukrainian war”.
The oil-rich nation of Libya has been divided between the government in Tripoli and a rival administration in the east since the overthrow of longtime ruler Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.

articles.title_orig: Hu Bo: Three Major Misunderstandings of China's Claims & Policies in South China Sea
articles.title_zh: Hu Bo: Three Major Misunderstandings of China's Claims & Policies in South China Sea
articles.content_orig:
Hu Bo , Director of the South China Sea Strategic Situation Probing Initiative (SCSPI) and Research Professor and Director of the Centre for Maritime Strategy Studies at Peking University, has argued that Beijing seeks to maintain rather than change the status quo in the South China Sea, and that every step taken by Beijing was a response to the Philippines.
The following is the transcript of Hu’s presentation at the 2026 Manila Dialogue on the South China Sea on November 17, 2026.
The video of Hu’s remarks is also available on SCSPI’s official YouTube channel. The transcript is based on this recording and has been lightly edited for clarity, with Hu's collaboration.
In these two days, we have heard a lot of China’s threat and China’s bullying. So let me tell you a different story.
Before we start, I think we should know that we are living in the international sovereignty system. International relation process is the circle of action and reaction. I would like to share three misunderstandings on China’s claims and China’s policies in the South China Sea.
The dash line, or the nine-dash line, just defines the scope of China’s claims in the South China Sea. It is not the legal basis for China’s claims.
If you notice China’s official statements, you will see that we have four kinds of claims.
The first claim is that China has sovereignty over four island groups including Paracel Islands and Spratly Islands and others, and this kind of sovereignty is based on international practice and the UN Charter. Many have been talking about distance, but distance has never been the legal basis for sovereignty claims.
Secondly, after the UNCLOS came into practice, China had a claim of territorial sea and 【Thirdly】EEZ (exclusive economic zone) generated by UNCLOS based on the four island groups.
Finally, China has historic rights in the South China Sea.
Beijing has never used the nine-dash line to claim 90% of the South China Sea as China’s territory. That’s fake news. I also want to remind Mr. Ray Powell that you couldn’t claim the sea as your territories. We just claimed the four island groups as our territories, inheriting the claims from the Republic of China.
Also, the arbitration ruling has stated that all features in the South China Sea couldn’t generate 200 miles of EEZ. We should know that even during the negotiation of the UNCLOS, after 10 years of negotiations involving thousands of representatives from more than 100 countries, no agreement could be reached on what kind of features could generate 200 miles of EEZ. How can five arbitrators decide that? Who gave them the courage?
As to the historic rights, there are also two Chinese academic debates on that. In order to save time, I will not interpret that. You can see it in this screen.
The second misunderstanding is that China restricts foreign maritime activities in our EEZ, but we don’t have this kind of law. In practice, we just intercept when foreign maritime activities approach too much on our territorial sea or airspace.
The third misunderstanding is that China wants to change the status quo. The real reality is that China wants to keep the status quo.
I think even now Beijing follows Deng Xiaoping’s principle of shelving disputes . We recognize that the occupation state in the Spratly Islands happened in history, and we would not use force to return them back. But we couldn’t accept new losses.
The Second Thomas Shoal is not on the occupation list that Beijing recognized. I will talk about it later.
China has never fired the first shot. Many of you are talking about the water cannon, but you may not know that China has never fired even a single bullet to our neighbour for more than three decades. But the Philippines shot down Chinese Taiwan fishermen in 2013. Also, there have been open-fire incidents happening among ASEAN member states. For instance, Vietnamese fishermen have had very bloody conflicts with law enforcement forces of Malaysia and Indonesia in recent years.
So, in this regard, I think China’s performance is much better than that of other claimants. We also emphasize the stability in the neighborhood relationship with their neighbors. But China is also a sovereign state. When facing challenges to its sovereignty and maritime rights, China has a reason to respond and must respond.
Under the current administration of the Philippines, ever since late 2022 and up to now, I think the Philippines has protested against Beijing more than 500 times, demanding that all Chinese presence — all the personnel and vessels — should leave the West Philippine Sea. It’s a very ambitious demand.
There are also the new EDCA (Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement) sites, especially two of them pointing towards Taiwan, as well as the Philippines’ high-level officers saying that the Philippines has 250,000 Filipinos in Taiwan, so Taiwan’s contingency is the Philippines’ contingency. If Beijing uses the same logic, we can say that we have a lot of Chinese citizens in the Philippines and we have a lot of economic interests in the Philippines. So, the Philippines’ contingency is China’s contingency. So, I think this kind of thing is totally nonsense.
Also, the Philippines has proposed to extend its continental shelf beyond the 200 miles of the EEZ.
And there are two laws, which I think is very important, to trigger China’s response on the Scarborough Shoal.
The current Philippine administration, from the beginning, denied any kind of “gentleman’s agreement” with Beijing, but this kind of gentleman’s agreement existed even during the Aquino III administration.
And the Philippines has shown the intention to occupy all the features in the West Philippine Sea.
In the following part, we will review the cases one by one. The first case is the Second Thomas Shoal.
The Philippines grounded [a ship in] the Second Thomas Shoal in 1999. At the beginning, the Philippines told Beijing that they were just temporarily grounded. But they continued to ground it in this feature. Before 2022, Beijing and Manila had some understanding and a gentleman’s agreement that ordinary resupply is no problem but no building materials.
But when this administration came into office, they denied this kind of arrangement. Also, they wanted to challenge China’s bottom line on the Second Thomas Shoal. The amount of building materials transported was around 10 tonnes. Beijing waited a long time, almost a year, to persuade the Philippines to change its course. Beijing responded to the Philippines operation only in August 2023. We waited a long time.
But after the incident on June 17 , I think the Philippines realised that they should have some mutual understanding with Beijing. So we have another, we could say, gentleman’s agreement on the resupply.
So, generally, I think the situation of the Second Thomas Shoal is calming down compared with other features. One thing I should say is that the Second Thomas Shoal is different from Thitu Island and the other seven features the Philippines occupied. Beijing has never recognised the occupation state of the Second Thomas Shoal.
This is the Sabina Shoal. I think the confrontation just came out in this current administration.
The heated period is between April and September 2024. But finally, I think Beijing and the Philippines both know that neither has the intention to occupy this feature. There have been some incidents even this year, but generally I think the tensions around Sabina Shoal has been decreased.
Beijing has never recognised that there was dispute in the Scarborough Shoal. Beijing just recognised that there are disputes in the Spratly Islands. That’s Beijing’s position.
And in the Scarborough Shoal, the incident happened in 2012. During that incident, the Philippine naval officers tortured Chinese fishermen in the lagoon of the Scarborough Shoal. Beijing responded by sending law enforcement vessels there. After the incident, Beijing was worrying about that the Philippines might repeat this

articles.title_orig: Braintree cat takes 74-mile round trip to London
articles.title_zh: Braintree cat takes 74-mile round trip to London
articles.content_orig:
A pet owner has thanked train staff for returning her adventure-loving cat after he made the commute from his Essex home town to central London.
Four-year-old Zeus caught the 20:08 from Braintree, on 10 November, and was intercepted by station staff 37 miles away (59km) at London Liverpool Street.
A Greater Anglia spokesperson said the half-British shorthair was taken to the staff office to keep him safe, before being escorted on his return trip back to Braintree.
"I just thought, 'oh my God, he's done it again'," said owner Lily Burroughs.
Zeus is no stranger to the railways, having previously made trips from his former home in Stansted Mountfitchet to London Stansted Airport.
Zeus, who used to be well-known for hanging out in his local Co-op, wears two trackers but his owner accepts his nomadic ways.
"I've tried to keep him in before and he just does himself damage, he's constantly trying to break out. He's just not happy being indoors all the time," said Burroughs.
"He's quite a social cat, he likes to see everyone so yeah without everyone else sort of looking out for him it would be a world of pain."
She continued: "Braintree to London is definitely the furthest that he's gone, but I think he would probably go further if he had the chance."
Burroughs thanked the "caring" staff who helped reunite the two of them.
The Greater Anglia spokesperson added: "Zeus enjoyed all the attention from staff at the station and customers on the train home."

articles.title_orig: Oil falls as robust Gulf exports offset Iran escalation, supply glut risks
articles.title_zh: Oil falls as robust Gulf exports offset Iran escalation, supply glut risks
articles.content_orig:
Oil prices fell slightly on Monday as investors focused on ⁠Middle East oil flows, with persistent shipping and refinery attacks in the Middle East offering support.
Brent crude futures ​fell 60 cents, ​or 0.65%, to $91.97 a ​barrel by 0844 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate futures were down 49 cents, or 0.59%, to $82.92 a barrel.
Brent declined 4% last week and WTI 5%.
The unresolved US-Israeli ⁠war ‌on Iran continued to support prices, however. On ⁠Sunday, the Iran-aligned Houthi movement said it attacked a Saudi Arabian oil refinery, while the UK Maritime Trade Operations reported multiple attacks on shipping in the Gulf and near the Strait of Hormuz ‌over the weekend.
"Oil recorded its third successive weekly loss, with pressure coming primarily from the supply side of the equation," said PVM analyst ​Tamas Varga.
"It would, nonetheless, be irresponsible to conclude that oil will now be supplied uninterruptedly and in vast volumes. Iranian attacks on ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz are taking their toll."
Bahrain said an Iranian ⁠attack hit a civilian industrial facility on Saturday, while Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they had launched ‌a missile-and-drone assault on US military positions in the ‌kingdom, home to the US Navy's 5th Fleet.
In Turkey, talks on Sunday at the global climate conference COP31 collapsed for the first time since 2009 after nations could not come ⁠to an agreement on including a statement on the phase-out of fossil ⁠fuels in a final text.
Saudi Arabia and other big oil-producing ⁠countries have said fossil fuels will play a role in the economy for the foreseeable future and they lobbied to keep any ​mention of fossil fuels out of the ‌text, observers at the conference said.
The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries had earlier defended fossil fuel use.
OPEC+ ministers will hold a series of meetings on November 29 to decide their 2027 output policy. The group is made up of OPEC and other ​oil producers such as Russia.

articles.title_orig: Ukrainian Drones Set Russian Oil Infrastructure Ablaze in Twin Strikes Deep Inside Russia
articles.title_zh: Ukrainian Drones Set Russian Oil Infrastructure Ablaze in Twin Strikes Deep Inside Russia
articles.content_orig:
In brief: The reported strikes targeted the Kaleykino pumping station, a key hub for Russia’s Druzhba oil pipeline, and the Novoshakhtinsk Oil Products Plant. Both facilities play a role in Russia’s oil supply and export infrastructure.
Ukrainian drones struck two Russian oil facilities early on Monday, Nov. 23, sparking major fires at a pumping station in Tatarstan and an oil refinery in the Rostov region, according to local residents and Russian media reports.
In Tatarstan, residents reported explosions and a large fire near the Kaleykino oil pumping station outside Almetyevsk.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The facility, located around 1,300 kilometers (808 miles) from the Ukrainian border, is a key hub in Russia’s oil transportation network and the starting point of the Druzhba pipeline.
The independent Russian outlet Astra identified the burning facility as the Kaleykino station based on videos shared by eyewitnesses.
The site was targeted less than a week earlier, on Thursday, Nov. 19, when local authorities claimed a major fire had been avoided. Officials have not commented on the latest reported attack.
Kaleykino receives, stores, and pumps crude from oil fields across Tatarstan, Western Siberia, Udmurtia, and Bashkortostan.
It feeds oil into Russia’s network of trunk pipelines, including the Druzhba route, supplying refineries and supporting export flows.
Meanwhile, explosions and a major fire were reported at the Novoshakhtinsk Oil Products Plant in Russia’s Rostov region.
Astra reported , citing eyewitness footage, that the fire may have affected both the refinery and the nearby premises of TATA-GAZ LLC, a private company involved in fuel trading, storage, and logistics.
The Novoshakhtinsk plant is a major refinery in southern Russia, owned by Yug Energo LLC. It is connected to the Sukhodolnaya-Rodionovskaya oil pipeline and operates an oil loading terminal in Rostov-on-Don, as well as a fleet for transporting petroleum products.
Rostov Region Governor Yury Slyusar confirmed a fire caused by falling drone debris but did not identify the affected facility. He claimed that more than 80 drones had been shot down over the region overnight.
The strikes come amid an intensified Ukrainian campaign against Russia’s oil industry, targeting refineries, storage facilities, and pipeline infrastructure used to supply the military and generate revenue for Moscow’s war effort.
Ukrainian forces have struck at least nine Russian refineries since late October, including five of the country’s largest oil-processing plants, according to Ukraine’s General Staff.
The latest wave of attacks has repeatedly hit major facilities in southern Russia. On Wednesday, Nov. 18, Ukrainian drones struck the Afipsky and Ilsky refineries in Krasnodar Krai for the second time that month.
Earlier attacks also targeted Russia’s second-largest oil refinery near St. Petersburg and the Omsk refinery in Siberia , some 2,500 kilometers (1,553 miles) from Ukraine.
The sustained campaign has contributed to a roughly 30% decline in Russian crude processing and fuel shortages in several regions, according to Ukrainian officials and industry estimates.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

articles.title_orig: Five takeaways from the failed climate talks COP31
articles.title_zh: Five takeaways from the failed climate talks COP31
articles.content_orig:
The COP31 summit in Turkey came as evidence of climate change could not have been clearer - 2026 bought glacier collapses, record European heat, and wildfires across Asia - but also when geopolitical divisions could not have been deeper.
The result was the longest-running climate talks in UN history failed to deliver on its central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts - to further climate action.
Despite two countries, Australia and Turkey, leading the charge in their joint hosting of the negotiations, they could not bring the nations together.
After a dramatic and fractious final day where countries walked out over the absence of mention of fossil fuels in the text and money issues, questions are being asked more loudly than ever before about whether the COP process can still deliver.
Here are five, key takeaways from the talks which the hosts hoped would become known as the "implementation COP".
This was the first COP since the UN warned that global temperatures are expected to exceed 1.5C degrees above pre-industrial levels. That is the threshold which countries agreed not to breach as part of the Paris Climate Agreement signed in 2015.
The draft agreement had acknowledged the uncomfortable reality that climate action to date has failed on its most crucial of targets.
Without agreement, that recognition has been lost.
Almost exactly a decade ago a group of the world's climate scientists - the official UN body the IPCC - warned what would happen if temperatures rose 1.5C vs 2C:
Throughout the talks and during the final day, many countries still acknowledged that the target remained their north star of climate action.
"This COP sought to confront hard truths – that global warming is set to overshoot 1.5C and that we must act with even more urgency to reduce emissions," said UK Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh at the close of the talks.
The draft had called for that overshoot to be kept as small and short-lived as possible – it also suggested something called carbon dioxide removal (CDR).
This is a process which takes greenhouse gases out of the atmosphere and has not been explicitly mentioned in a COP final agreement before.
Carbon dioxide can be removed naturally by planting trees - although there are limits to the scale and permanence of that.
There are other technological solutions, but these are controversial and are not well advanced.
This year's negotiations have exposed a troubling problem - consensus does not last forever.
On the central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts – countries could not bridge the divide on including language on fossil fuels.
And yet the very same pledge had been made just three years ago at COP28 in Dubai.
Rich nations also failed to put a figure to how much more money could be given to developing countries to adapt to climate change.
This is despite there already being a commitment from last year to triple the figure by 2035 from $40bn (£30bn) - but the interpretation of that pledge remains contested.
If governments cannot even agree to reaffirm commitments they've already made, it raises troubling questions about their ability to work together as the climate crisis intensifies.
Minister Chris Bowen from Australia, who was co-leading the negotiations, pointed out at the end of the talks that the world is a very different place from when these commitments were struck just a few years ago.
"The situation coming into this COP was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory".
That was made apparent during the final meeting when pointed remarks were delivered. EU representative Darragh O'Brien said the talks had been "hijacked by some oil states".
Russian delegate Sergei Kononuchenko switched from Russian to English to directly address the EU delegation. He accused them of providing climate finance only in the form of loans to developing nations: "This is an old colonial distribution of labour under a new banner".
It is a serious blow not just to climate action, but to multilateralism itself - the idea that countries can put aside their differences on other issues to tackle problems they can't solve alone.
Much of the coverage of COP31 has focused on the failure to get the central political agreement passed.
But much of the work at these summits is putting into action agreements made at previous meetings.
On money that is going towards adaptation for example, countries need to agree how is it being distributed, is it making an impact and how can this be tracked, and which areas are particularly vulnerable.
In fact, there were 164 other items on this year's agenda that were being thrashed out in the negotiating rooms.
And some of those were agreed at the talks.
The funds raised from a global system of carbon credits – money given in exchange for releasing greenhouse gases – will go towards helping developing countries adapt to the impacts of climate change.
They agreed to advance a just transition framework designed to protect workers and communities as global economies shift toward clean energy.
But there were many more that could not be agreed and some will now be picked up at COP32, including crucially the work programme responsible for driving forward action on cutting emissions.
What governments agree in the COP negotiating rooms is only part of what determines the speed of the energy transition.
The International Energy Agency's latest World Energy Outlook points to another powerful force: energy security.
It says the disruption to oil and gas supplies through the Strait of Hormuz has been the biggest energy supply shock in history. The longer the uncertainty continues, the stronger the incentive for countries to switch from imported fossil fuels to electricity generated at home.
The economics have been changing too.
Solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles have become increasingly competitive.
As clean energy develops its own commercial momentum, formal negotiations may become less important in determining its direction and pace.
Against the headwinds of inflation new investment announcements emerged at COP as part of the "Action Agenda".
This is the part of the COP process that tries to mobilise action outside of formal talks from businesses, investors and cities – this year the focus was on electrification. Turning more of our energy from fossil fuels to electricity.
"We are not entering the age of electricity, we have arrived at the age of electricity," Fatih Birol, head of the IEA, told the BBC. He says energy security and climate policies are now "closely aligned".
That doesn't make COP irrelevant.
Governments still have a crucial role in facilitating the transition, according to Dr Jennie Dodson, a senior director at the World Business Council for Sustainable Development which includes among its members the likes of Amazon and Apple.
"A key message from business is we can go so far, a lot of it is cost competitive, but there are policy barriers both around infrastructure and permitting".
COP31 has shown how the role of these annual UN climate conferences is changing.
For the first 30 COPs, the emphasis was on building the international framework for tackling global warming.
The great diplomatic breakthrough came in Paris in 2015, when almost every country agreed to keep global warming well below 2°C and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C.
Paris also established machinery designed to turn promises into progress. Every five years, governments assess collective progress in a global stocktake and submit new national climate plans, known as NDCs.
Then came further agreements: a fund for climate damage at COP27, a commitment to transition away from fossil fuels and triple renewable energy capacity at COP28, a new climate finance target at COP29 and increased support for adaptation at COP30.
The international architecture for tackling climate change has, in other words, largely been built.

articles.title_orig: Iranian president turns out office lights to urge citizens to save energy
articles.title_zh: Iranian president turns out office lights to urge citizens to save energy
articles.content_orig:
Truck drivers in several Iranian cities have gone on strike over rising operating costs, stagnant freight rates and worsening economic conditions, with reports of work stoppages emerging on Sunday.
A video sent to Iran International showed a group of truck drivers stopping work in Shiraz, southern Iran, on Sunday.
The Telegram channel of the Union of Truck Drivers and Trucking Associations Across Iran also reported strikes in several cities, including Chabahar in southeastern Iran’s Sistan and Baluchestan Province and Dezful in southwestern Khuzestan Province, citing messages from its members.
“We went on strike because of these incompetent officials who do not care about the country or its people. We cannot go on like this anymore,” one driver wrote in a message to the union.
Another driver pointed to soaring truck maintenance costs, saying 40 liters of engine oil and five filters now cost 620 million rials (approximately $230 at the free-market exchange rate).
For comparison, Iran’s minimum monthly wage in 2026 is about 166 million rials ($62), meaning the maintenance bill is equivalent to nearly four months of base pay for a minimum-wage worker.
A third driver urged colleagues to remain patient, arguing that the effects of a transport strike would take more than 24 or 48 hours to become visible.
“Be patient. Produce markets will empty, ports will empty, and factories will come to a halt,” the driver said.
The Union of Truck Drivers and Trucking Associations Across Iran announced its full support for a nationwide strike on Saturday, November 21, calling on drivers across the country to stop work from November 22.
The union said freight rates had remained unchanged despite sharp increases in the prices of engine oil, tires and spare parts.
It also cited rising fuel, insurance, toll and repair costs, along with job insecurity and insufficient support for drivers, as reasons for the strike.
“This strike is a cry of protest from drivers who have spent years struggling under the weight of rising prices, injustice and neglect and can no longer endure these unbearable conditions,” the union said in its statement.
The strikes come as Iran faces renewed electricity outages and reports of long queues at petrol stations in several cities.
The continuation of the protests could encourage other professional groups to join, political analyst Iman Aghayari said in an interview with Iran International.
The authorities are concerned about the potential spread of protests and are seeking to prevent other sections of society from joining through threats, inducements and repression, Aghayari added.
Iran's worsening economic conditions have placed growing pressure on households, particularly workers and pensioners struggling to meet everyday expenses.
An investigation by Iran International found dealers offering firearms through social media and messaging platforms, with some claiming they could deliver weapons anywhere in the country within two weeks.
The sellers describe a market shaped by financial hardship, fears of insecurity and demand from people seeking weapons to threaten or intimidate others.
But the scale of the trade remains unclear, as does how many advertised weapons actually change hands.
Who buys and sells guns in Iran?
One arms dealer told Iran International that some of his suppliers were livestock farmers, nomads and villagers who had owned rifles for years, including Brno, M1 and various shotguns.
Some legally possessed their weapons but had decided to sell them because of financial difficulties and rising living costs, he said.
Others owned unlicensed firearms, particularly military-style weapons, and feared their children or other family members might use them.
The dealer said he purchased weapons from their owners and resold them at a profit.
One seller said concerns about theft and personal security had prompted some wealthy Iranians to purchase firearms to protect themselves and their property.
Other customers, he claimed, were involved in illegal economic activities and sought weapons to collect debts, intimidate others or settle financial disputes.
From handguns to Kalashnikovs
Prices vary widely depending on the type, condition and country of manufacture of a weapon.
According to sellers interviewed by Iran International, prices for licensed Iranian-made firearms start at around 300 million tomans.
Handguns described as Turkish or Pakistani start at approximately 500 million rials, while weapons advertised as Beretta or Glock models can cost as much as $5,000.
One dealer quoted around 2 billion rials for a secondhand Chinese-made Kalashnikov, compared with as much as 8 billion rials for a Russian-made equivalent.
Ammunition is sold separately, with dealers quoting approximately 4,000,000 rials for a Kalashnikov cartridge and 8,000,000 rials for a Brno rifle cartridge.
These are asking prices rather than independently verified completed transactions.
Social media advertisements examined by Iran International featured photographs and videos of firearms, accompanied by model names and prices.
One dealer claimed he could deliver weapons to different parts of Iran in less than 15 days. Another confirmed that delivery to Tehran was possible.
Some sellers demanded full payment before shipment, while others accepted deposits and the balance upon delivery.
One dealer claimed to have contacts with wholesale arms suppliers in Iraq's Kurdistan Region, allowing him to obtain different models from across the border. He promised refunds if a weapon could not be delivered.
Another seller said neither a buyer's identity nor the intended use of a weapon mattered to him. Once payment was received, he said, the firearm would be dispatched.
A market vulnerable to fraud
The proliferation of online gun advertisements has raised questions about how many sellers are genuine.
In a separate investigation conducted last year, reporters contacted five sellers advertising firearms through Telegram channels, but none provided a way to verify that they possessed the weapons on offer.
Two sent identical responses and price lists, raising questions about whether some advertisements were fraudulent or relied on common promotional templates.
Iranian police have reported operations against networks advertising and selling firearms online.
In early November, police announced that they had identified an online firearms distribution channel and seized two military-style handguns during an operation against suspects.
3D-printed guns enter the picture
The investigation also identified advertisements offering small, single-shot firearms described as having been manufactured using 3D printers.
Some have plastic bodies and unconventional shapes that can make them resemble toys, while their manufacture does not necessarily require industrial production facilities or the importation of complete firearms.
However, there is no reliable information about the number of producers in Iran, the volume of sales or the performance of the advertised models.
The emergence of such weapons has raised concerns internationally, with European researchers reporting increasingly sophisticated 3D-printed firearms and growing numbers of seizures.
Official figures show thousands of illegal firearms being seized across Iran, although they offer only a partial picture of the market.
Police spokesman Saeed Montazerolmahdi said in November that firearms seizures had increased by 14% through the end of the Iranian month of Mehr, compared with the corresponding period a year earlier.
He said military-style weapons accounted for 31% of the firearms seized, with seizures in that category rising by 9%.
A review of police and judicial announcements across several provinces, alongside border enforcement reports, produced a combined total exceeding 12,300 firearms.
The figures cover different reporting periods and may overlap, meaning the total does not necessarily represent 12,300 separate weapons.

articles.title_orig: 'As soon as I work, I get penalised - I fear I will never own my own home'
articles.title_zh: 'As soon as I work, I get penalised - I fear I will never own my own home'
articles.content_orig:
A disabled man fears he will never be able to own his own home because of limits on how much he can save due to social care rules.
Maxwell McKnight, from St Neots, has spinal muscular atrophy and receives direct payments from Cambridgeshire County Council for his care.
He works full-time in a graduate-level job and is saving for a house deposit. However, the adult social care upper capital limit is £23,250, meaning anything he manages to save above that limit will go towards his care instead.
His case was highlighted in Parliament by MP Ian Sollom. Prime Minister Andy Burnham called the situation "unfair" and asked for it to be looked into.
The Department for Health and Social Care (DHSC) said it wanted to "support people to live independently and participate fully in society".
McKnight recently graduated from Anglia Ruskin University with a first-class degree in Business Management. He now works as a marketing executive.
However, he said his earnings limit the various forms of help and support he can apply for and how much he receives.
"As soon as I work, I'm getting penalised for that; it's almost like I would be better off not working," he said.
"It is so bizarre because the government want disabled people to work... I just think that's really unfair.
"I feel like I've done everything right in life, you know, I've got the degree, I've gone to work, and now my ambitions are kind of being stopped... by the government, because of the upper capital limit."
His story was raised at Prime Minister's Questions by MP Ian Sollom.
The Liberal Democrat member for St Neots and Mid Cambridgeshire said the cap was "placing a limit on the aspirations of young people".
Andy Burnham said McKnight's case was "very powerful" and "unfair". He said he would like to see the issue presented to Baroness Casey, who is currently conducting a review into adult social care.
Sollom said he would also continue to do what he could.
"Young people like Maxwell have done everything the government has asked of them under difficult circumstances – studied, worked hard, paid tax – and yet they are being punished by a savings trap, which has not been changed for over 15 years," he said.
"There are credible solutions out there that would free young people from a lifetime of expensive care costs.
"I am calling on the health secretary to engage with disabled young people like Maxwell and urgently put forward solutions."
DHSC added: "From April this year, we increased the Minimum Income Guarantee for working-age adults by up to 7% – the biggest above-inflation uplift in over a decade – benefiting more than 150,000 people and providing an average cash boost of around £400 a year.
"Baroness Casey's commission on the future of adult social care is also examining how we can make the system fairer and more supportive for individuals of all ages who are in need of care, and we have brought forward her final report to next summer so we can act as quickly as possible on her recommendations for reform."
Local authorities carry out a financial assessment for direct payment and other support, and the government said not all forms of income were taken into account as part of this.
Cambridgeshire County Council was contacted for comment.

articles.title_orig: Woman at center of Nvidia scandal was in touch with China's top spy agency: Sources - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Woman at center of Nvidia scandal was in touch with China's top spy agency: Sources - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Alice Huang, the alleged spy at the center of the Nvidia scandal, was in touch with an official from China's top spy agency during an affair with the chip giant's former chief executive Jensen Huang, the New York Times reported on Sunday.
Alice Huang was this month outed as a suspected Chinese spy, accused of having an affair with Jensen Huang while digging up company secrets for Beijing.
She was in contact with an officer of China's Ministry of State Security from the spring of 2025 until the fall of this year, the Times reported, citing people with knowledge of the intelligence.
Alice Huang, who is no relation to Jensen, previously led Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based tech group under investigation for allegedly helping Chinese firms gain access to Nvidia chips, possibly in violation of US export controls.
According to the Times, Alice Huang's contacts with the Chinese spy agency correspond to the affair as well as a period when Megaspeed was acquiring large amounts of advanced Nvidia chips.
The Times also reported that US intelligence agencies have gathered evidence that Alice Huang's business partner Kang Wei -- who the newspaper said was often introduced as her husband -- worked with the same Chinese spy agency.
Jensen Huang stepped down as Nvidia's chief executive earlier this month, following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with Alice Huang.
He is to be questioned by US lawmakers on December 1 over national security concerns.
The upheaval has battered shares of Nvidia which is at the center of an AI boom that has helped propel markets to record highs and boosted economic growth around the globe.

articles.title_orig: Investigation: How Russians with criminal records obtained Romanian passports by posing as Ukrainians
articles.title_zh: Investigation: How Russians with criminal records obtained Romanian passports by posing as Ukrainians
articles.content_orig:
Russian citizens, including those linked to Russia’s war machine and terrorist groups, can travel and operate freely within the EU with their new Romanian passports.
The Kyiv Independent investigation reveals how Russian citizens obtained EU passports by posing as Ukrainians. (Nataliia Shulga / The Kyiv Independent)
Editor's note: This investigation is a collaboration between the Kyiv Independent, Public Record (Romania), Cu Sens (Moldova), Follow the Money (the Netherlands), Le Monde (France), and the Investigative Center of Ján Kuciak (Slovakia).
Hundreds of new Romanian citizens are not Romanian at all.
In recent years, hundreds of foreigners — many of them Russians — have exploited Bucharest's repatriation process to obtain authentic Romanian passports via forged citizenship certificates, according to Romanian authorities.
A Romanian passport comes with EU citizenship — and a right to live, work, and travel visa-free across the continent and beyond.
These suspect identity records are now being challenged in court in civil lawsuits, while law enforcement simultaneously pursues a large criminal investigation to uncover the organized groups behind the fraudulent document scheme.
The Kyiv Independent and its partner newsrooms in five countries reviewed civil court records for 55 people who, according to Romanian authorities, obtained genuine Romanian birth certificates using forged papers. More than 30 of them turned out to be Russian citizens. At least some of them, this investigation found, went on to obtain Romanian passports.
For Russian citizens who have never enjoyed visa-free travel in Europe — and were hit with new visa restrictions after the start of the full-scale invasion — Romanian passports offered a way to evade sanctions and access the privileges of the EU.
To obtain these valuable documents, some Russians even pretended to be Ukrainians. This investigation found eight cases where Russian citizens used questionable Ukrainian passports and fake Romanian citizenship certificates to obtain authentic Romanian identity documents in 2023 and 2024 — during Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine.
Among the Russians who posed as Ukrainians on their way to EU passports, the Kyiv Independent identified a member of a powerful clan in Chechnya , the then-head of a Russian state-owned explosives manufacturer, and a man named in reports linking him to organized crime.
Fraudulent schemes to obtain Romanian passports exploit a legitimate legal route to citizenship.
Romania offers repatriation to descendants of people who lost their citizenship against their will. Most of them lived in regions the country lost in 1940, and which are now part of Moldova and Ukraine .
If a person can prove their familial link to these lost lands, they have a right to a Romanian citizenship certificate.
The fraud lies in the documents used to claim this right.
Such schemes typically begin with a forged genealogy document, likely issued in a third country, that links the applicant to ancestors from former Romanian territories.
Previous findings by Romanian prosecutors showed that Russians, Ukrainians, and Moldovans have used forged genealogy documents to obtain genuine Romanian citizenship certificates.
In more recent cases, prosecutors say, the citizenship certificates themselves have been forged. This shortcut can shave years off the application process and, crucially, bypasses criminal background checks.
The fraudsters then use the forged citizenship certificate to obtain a series of authentic Romanian identity documents: a birth certificate transcribed into the Romanian civil registry, an ID card, and a passport.
The fraudulent networks rely on middlemen and Romanian clerks, and they may operate behind a seemingly legitimate public face: private migration agencies, whose ads have flooded Russian social media since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the tightening of EU visa rules for Russian citizens.
According to a Romanian lawyer who has represented clients in dozens of annulment cases in Romania, the fake citizenship scheme can cost between roughly 50,000 and 70,000 euros ($55,000 to $77,000) per person. The lawyer spoke to Le Monde on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the subject.
Eight Russian citizens, including a sanctioned defense-industry executive and a man linked to organized crime, obtained Romanian documents using questionable Ukrainian identity papers.
The annulment lawsuits filed by Romanian authorities list each person’s date and place of birth and their parents’ names, details that helped the Kyiv Independent identify them.
One is Mairbek Abdulazizov, a member of a family at the heart of the regime of Chechen dictator Ramzan Kadyrov , the warlord who has called himself "Putin's foot soldier." Kadyrov’s forces have fought in Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and Ukrainian prosecutors have brought multiple war crimes charges against Kadyrov and his fighters.
In Chechnya, Mairbek Abdulazizov advises the director of the Regional Compulsory Health Insurance Fund. This happens to be his own brother, Denilbek Abdulazizov, who has run the fund since 2007, when Kadyrov formally came to power.
The fund controls the money for Chechnya’s state-funded health care and, according to the Russian outlet Novaya Gazeta , serves as a channel for large, opaque financial flows in the region.
In 2024, Kadyrov awarded Mairbek Abdulazizov the Order of Kadyrov, Chechnya's highest state award.
The Abdulazizovs keep power in the family. Another brother, Sharpudi Abdulazizov, is Chechnya’s environment minister, and a nephew, Turpal-Ali Abdulazizov, heads the administration of the family’s native Vedensky district.
Another Russian named in the Romanian files is Dmitrii Rudenko, who spent more than a decade in Moscow's defense industry.
Until April 2025, he headed the state-owned Special Design and Technological Bureau Tekhnolog, which develops explosives for Russian tank ammunition and missile systems. In October 2026, the EU added the bureau to its sanctions list, citing its role in Russia's military-industrial complex. Ukraine sanctioned both the bureau and Rudenko in 2023.
While Rudenko worked in Russia’s defense industry, his family appears to have been building a life in Europe — despite Russia’s anti-Western rhetoric, it’s a common feature of many wealthy Russian families linked to the country’s war effort. He has traveled to France repeatedly since 2022 and transferred at least 700,000 euros abroad, Russian media reported, citing investigators.
Documents obtained by Le Monde, a partner in this investigation, show that Rudenko's former wife, Natalia Zelentsova, bought two apartments in Beausoleil in 2014 and 2015, while still officially married to him. The couple divorced in 2017 but kept traveling together, according to leaked Russian customs and flight records.
In October 2022, months after Russia launched its full-scale invasion, Zelentsova reportedly applied for asylum or residency in France, and she has not returned to Russia since. Rudenko’s son from a previous marriage, Andrey, is listed in the French telephone directory at the building where, according to French property records, Zelentsova owns two apartments.
Rudenko's position in Russia has also become precarious. In February 2025, he was arrested on charges of embezzlement and money laundering. No further details of his case have been made public.
Another name in the files points to Russia's criminal underworld.
Nurutdin Dadaev, a Russian citizen from Dagestan , landed on Ukraine’s sanctions list in 2021 along with his brother. Ukrainian media reported that the list targeted so-called “thieves in law,” the elites of the post-Soviet criminal world. Russia itself had already flagged Dadaev: in 2020, its financial crime watchdog added him to its list of terrorists and extremists.

articles.title_orig: Beatles venue may not play live music on rooftop
articles.title_zh: Beatles venue may not play live music on rooftop
articles.content_orig:
Plans to create a museum where The Beatles performed their last live performance is expected to be approved - but on condition no live music can be played on the rooftop that made the Mayfair venue famous.
Apple Corps Ltd, the company founded by the band, wants to convert 3 Savile Row into a seven-floor "cultural experience and exhibition" celebrating The Beatles, with a basement café-bar on the site of the studio where Let It Be was recorded in 1969.
The Beatles famously stunned locals in January 1969 by playing a set on the roof of the Grade II* listed building, which was Apple Corps' headquarters.
Westminster City councillors are due to vote on the plans on Tuesday.
The council papers set out for the first time the scale of the attraction Sir Paul McCartney announced in May .
Apple Corps is forecasting up to 900 visitors each weekday and 1,140 on weekends, entering in timed slots of 20 people every 10 minutes.
There is a proposed limit of 225 visitors at any one time.
The basement café/bar would open until midnight seven nights a week, and events would be capped at 104 a year, averaging two events a week.
The draft conditions also state that no live music can be played on the terrace and any amplified music or speech should be noise limited. A two-metre-high acoustic barrier has also been proposed.
The Savile Row Bespoke Association, which represents the street's bespoke tailors, has objected to the plans stating they are in conflict with the Savile Row Special Policy Area planning designation that aims to protect bespoke tailoring on the street.
It has also warned that narrow pavements "would lead to dangerous congestion and have a significant negative impact on those who visit and work on Savile Row".
The Mayfair Neighbourhood Forum has not objected in principle but said visitor numbers "need to be greatly reduced" and asked for the operation to be monitored for 12 months before any expansion.
Planning officers state "the proposal does not comply wholly" with the Special Policy Area but say the building's unique link to The Beatles justifies an exception.
They have suggested a clause that would require the building to revert to its previous office or retail use if the venue closed.
Announcing the plans in May, Sir Paul told the BBC that tourists "come to England and they can go to Abbey Road, but they can't go inside" and described the Savile Row project as "a terrific idea".
He said visitors would "work your way up through the building… until you get to the top, where you go out on the roof and pretend to be a Beatle".
The Beatles at 3 Savile Row is due to open in 2027, if planning permission is obtained.

articles.title_orig: US intelligence chief warns of more tech outages as Delta suffers fresh Atlanta failure
articles.title_zh: US intelligence chief warns of more tech outages as Delta suffers fresh Atlanta failure
articles.content_orig:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Americans to prepare for "bumps in the road" after a set of damaging technology outages rocked air travel and systems like Microsoft Outlook.
Government officials have largely dismissed the prospects that the outages, which also slowed bank transactions , are linked to a coordinated or artificial intelligence cyberattack.
Clayton, however, said on CNN's "State of the Union" that outages may continue as companies and the government upgrade their systems to adapt to the AI age.
"The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road," Clayton said.
"You prepare by knowing that systems are going to be upgraded; they may be interrupted for a period of time and that companies and government are dealing with this on the front foot," he said.
Clayton's warning came as the U.S. prepares to celebrate Thanksgiving on Thursday, one of the busiest travel weeks of the year. A technology outage prompted a nationwide ground stop just over a week ago, which lasted for hours.
The Federal Aviation Administration said router upgrades caused a flood of data that led to the ground stop, and that there is no indication of a cyberattack.
Separately, Microsoft said the Outlook outage was caused by "an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade."
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent delivered a similar message on CBS' "Face the Nation."
Asked if Americans should be concerned about the security of their financial institutions, Bessent said: "No, they shouldn't."
"The patches may cause a glitch," he said, referring to measures banks are taking to safeguard from AI. "I think the American people should think of it as a vaccine; your arm may hurt, you may feel a little bad the next day, but it increases your long-term immunity and resiliency."

articles.title_orig: Copper Wavers Near $12,000 a Ton After Meltdown on AI Jitters
articles.title_zh: Copper Wavers Near $12,000 a Ton After Meltdown on AI Jitters
articles.content_orig:
It has been a difficult week for metals. Copper is down more than 8%, aluminium almost 6% and gold around 9% as a stronger dollar, higher rate expectations and weaker risk appetite weigh on the complex
The speed of the sell-off looks more like a sharp repricing of investor exposure than a broad weakening in physical markets . Copper has taken the biggest hit as investors unwind bullish positions and reassess AI-related demand. Yet the sharp correction in prices contrasts with still-tight physical markets.
Copper is on track for one of its steepest weekly declines in a decade.
We think the speed of the sell-off partly reflects an unwind of bullish investor positioning. Both LME and COMEX net length have fallen sharply from recent highs, while positioning across the wider metals complex has also become less bullish.
Copper has also become more closely correlated with equity markets, including AI-related stocks. The AI link matters for investor sentiment, but it does not make copper's demand story dependent on data centres alone. Grid investment and electrification remain important sources of demand. But as investors cut exposure to AI-related assets, copper has become more vulnerable to the same selling pressure.
That contrasts sharply with the physical market in China. Shanghai inventories are at their lowest since late 2023, while the Yangshan premium reached a record $500/t this week.
Bloomberg reports that some US copper is now being offered to buyers in China, where physical availability remains tight. Volumes are limited so far, but the shift raises the possibility that some of the metal accumulated in the US ahead of potential tariffs could start returning to the global market.
Copper could remain under pressure if funds continue to cut positions or the macro backdrop deteriorates. But the price correction has moved much faster than physical conditions. Tight availability in China should provide some support once the investor selling eases.
The risk is that more US metal returns to the wider market if tariff expectations fade further, gradually easing some of the regional tightness now supporting the physical market.
Aluminium has fallen with the wider complex, but nearby supply remains tight. The LME cash-to-three-month spread has moved into a steep backwardation, while LME stocks remain historically low and largely of Russian origin, limiting what is readily available to some buyers. This should help contain the near-term downside.
At the same time, investors have reduced bullish aluminium positions from recent highs, in line with the broader move across metals.
The medium-term picture is less supportive. Middle Eastern production is recovering, and new Indonesian capacity is coming online. We expect the market to move towards surplus next year, which should limit the scope for a sustained price recovery.
Gold has fallen for five straight sessions and is down around 9% this week, putting it on course for its steepest weekly decline since March. Prices have also touched their lowest level since September 2025.
The shift in the macro backdrop has weighed on gold, with higher rate expectations and a stronger dollar reducing its appeal. The equity sell-off may also have prompted some investors to sell gold to raise cash.
We expect gold to remain vulnerable while rate expectations and the dollar remain elevated. Central bank demand remains an important longer-term support, with China adding 26 tonnes to its reserves in October. But for now, macro forces are likely to set the direction.

articles.title_zh: Boy, 7, pulled alive from rubble hours after Russian strike on Ukraine, rescuers say
articles.content_orig:
Woman and child pulled out alive after overnight strike in Dymer north of Kyiv; UN mission calls for investigation into attack that sank Russian warship in Libya. What we know on day 1,734
Rescuers in Ukraine raced on Monday to find residents trapped under the rubble of a block of flats that partially collapsed in a Russian strike, after overnight attacks on the Kyiv region killed at least 14 people . A strike on Dymer, about 45km north of the capital, hit a five-storey building, killing at least 11, according to Kyiv regional official Tymur Tkachenko. He gave the latest toll while saying rescuers ‌had pulled another body ​from the ⁠rubble. The dead included a teenager and a woman in her 40s, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service (SES) said earlier. Tkachenko said rescuers also pulled out people alive from the rubble including a child and a 79-year-old woman. The SES said earlier it was searching for 11 people, including two children, who were “not responding or cannot be reached”. “When [the explosion came], I literally flipped over in bed,” said Mykola Osadnyi, a relative of some of the missing who lived nearby. “My father-in-law … was screaming: ‘Save me, I’m burning!’” Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets called the attack part of “Russia’s genocidal war against Ukraine”.
In Vyshneve, three people were killed and 15 wounded – including three children – when a Russian strike hit a supermarket , mayor Illya Dikov said. “People had simply gone to the store to buy groceries,” Tkachenko said. One more person was killed when a strike set a private home ablaze in Bila Tserkva, he added. Russia also struck a power substation in the Dnipropetrovsk region, Ukrainian prime minister Sergiy Koretsky said on social media.
A Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was struck early on Sunday in a suspected Ukrainian sea drone attack , causing a dramatic night-time explosion and the sinking of the vessel. The strike – more than 1,000 miles from southern Ukraine – severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette that had stopped to refuel and take on supplies, according to Libyan officials from the country’s eastern government, report Dan Sabbagh and Angelique Chrisafis . Hours later, a Russia-linked cargo ship said to be carrying military supplies was hit by a sea drone off the coast of Benghazi. There was no immediate reaction from Russian authorities and no immediate claim of responsibility for the strike. The UN mission in Libya (Unsmil) expressed “serious concern” over the drone attacks and called for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”, in a post on X.
Polish authorities say they have identified three flying objects that hit the country’s south-east as Russian cruise missiles, as Nato prepared to meet about an incident that Polish prime minister Donald Tusk called an “intentional provocation” . The prosecutor’s office in the city of Lublin said on Sunday that examination of fragments of the missiles that fell on Friday in the villages of Nowy Lipowiec, Rudnik and Molodycz showed they were all Russian Kh-101 missiles. No one was injured when the missiles hit, though one impact was followed by an explosion and fire. Nato allies will meet in Brussels on Monday to discuss the incident. The missiles fell close to where thousands of troops from the European “coalition of the willing” – set up to support Ukraine – were holding exercises.
Denmark has expelled a Russian official after it said it had thwarted an alleged plot to kill a Ukrainian American rapper at a concert on Danish soil. The case took a new twist on Sunday when Polish authorities revealed that the same man, Albert Vasiliev, was allegedly targeted by Moscow’s intelligence services last summer in Poland. Denmark is reportedly expected to ask the European Union this week for more decisive action stemming from the case.

articles.title_orig: Shopify CEO says Jensen Huang's ouster was 'choreographed' and calls Nvidia board ‘knuckleheads’
articles.title_zh: Shopify CEO says Jensen Huang's ouster was 'choreographed' and calls Nvidia board ‘knuckleheads’
articles.content_orig:
Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke had some strong words about Nvidia's board over its handling of Jensen Huang's resignation.
In an episode of David Senra's podcast released Sunday, Lütke questioned the sequence of allegations that preceded Huang's departure, saying it appeared too neatly arranged to be incidental.
"Let's be honest, this was surgical: affair, Chinese spy, another affair, another affair," Lütke said. "This is, like, choreographed. It's too organized. This is exactly how you write it in a book as a takedown story."
Huang stepped down as Nvidia CEO this month after an affair scandal and an investigation into concerns that he may have been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. Nvidia has said Huang voluntarily resigned after disclosures of conduct inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms. The board is not considering reinstating him, Business Insider reported last week.
On the podcast, Lütke said he could be wrong and that Huang may have had the alleged affairs. Still, Lütke said there was a "pretty large list" of people who stood to benefit from Huang no longer having his job. He did not name any people or organizations.
Lütke also called Nvidia's board "knuckleheads" and said that the company was at risk of becoming a legacy company because of what he described as the board's snap decision during the scandal.
He added that there was no track record of "custodian" CEOs successfully managing companies as "red hot" as Nvidia.
"You can put him on administrative leave or figure out something, but he built this company," he said.
He added, "The burden of proof needs to be much, much, much higher for saying that he's not the right person to run this company."
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
The German-Canadian entrepreneur co-founded Shopify in September 2004, became its CEO in 2008, and has led the company through its evolution into one of the world's largest e-commerce platforms.
Lütke, like several tech leaders , has consistently supported Huang since the scandal broke. On November 12, he called Huang's departure a "generational blunder" based on the information available at the time, writing that "there is no replacing a founder like Jensen" and that Nvidia would become a company "cosplaying Nvidia" under custodial management.

articles.title_orig: China Fears A.I. Could Give the U.S. an Edge in Nuclear Rivalry
articles.title_zh: China Fears A.I. Could Give the U.S. an Edge in Nuclear Rivalry
articles.content_orig:
Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney shakes hands with China's President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit on Nov. 19, 2026.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is placing particular focus on renewing relations with China as he aims to deepen international trade ties and diversify from U.S. reliance amid a three-month-long trade war with the U.S.
When asked what cards Canada holds in its ongoing talks with Washington, Carney, who recently announced a new partnership with the E.U. , pointed to the country's budding relationships elsewhere.
“Our cards are that everyone else in the world wants to deal with us,” he said Wednesday during a remote interview with the New York Times from Shenzhen, China, where he was among the world leaders attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit . "If the U.S. doesn't want to do the deal, we're busy.” His remarks came in the wake of President Donald Trump's claim that the U.S. holds “all the cards” after trade talks collapsed in August, leading to both sides enforcing heavy retaliatory tariffs .
Carney and Trump had a meeting on the sidelines of APEC, but aside from a commitment to “continue” negotiations and stay in close contact, no progress was made. However, Carney painted his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in a much more positive light. Ahead of the summit, Carney and Xi announced a Canada-China trade pact , which provided additional tariff relief on Canadian food and agricultural exports into China, and in return saw Canada agree to extend tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by two years.
Carney, who is promoting a “Canada Strong” platform as he aims to build economic resilience at home, touted the expansion of the trade arrangement with China as something that will deliver “greater certainty and prosperity for all Canadians.” He also praised the negotiation process with China, saying: “They’re very professional. They move forward in a very linear fashion.”
In an eight-day tour that took him from a European summit in Ireland to the Philippines, Cambodia, and finally China for the APEC gathering, Carney forged ahead with his plan to diversify Canada's economy away from its dependence on the U.S., which by far remains the country's largest trading partner .
Experts say Canada's progress in deepening its economic relationships with China could challenge Trump's insistence that Washington holds the upper hand in trade negotiations.
“Part of the Trump Administration’s [belief] is that everybody needs the U.S. more than anything else, and therefore the U.S. has maximum leverage,” says Jennifer Hillman, co-director of the Institute of International Economic Law at Georgetown University. “What this is clearly saying is that Canada can afford to be less willing to give the U.S. whatever it asks for [in negotiations], because they have other options.”
China has the world's second-largest economy , behind only the U.S., giving it the potential to become a much larger market for Canadian goods than some of the other countries Carney has sought to deepen relations with.
“China represents a very big market and the potential of a really big trading partner,” says Lori Turnbull, a professor in the Faculty of Management at Dalhousie University, noting it could be a leverage point in U.S. negotiations. “Doing a deal with a country like China is something that [the U.S.] will care about because of the size of China's economy and its competitive relationship with the U.S.”
Carney's latest push to strengthen trade ties with Beijing forms part of a months-long effort to renew Canada-China relations. In January, he met with Xi to forge what he called a “ new strategic partnership ,” agreeing to allow in up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles at a tariff of 6.1%, rather than the previous 100% levy. China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola seeds, a major Canadian export.
The move drew criticism from Trump, who said that “China will eat Canada alive, completely devour it, including the destruction of their businesses, social fabric, and general way of life.”
While Canada's closer relationship with China could strengthen its hand in negotiations, experts also warn that it could backfire.
Turnbull points to the latest agreement to extend tariff exemptions on Chinese steel and aluminum as a potential source of tension with Washington. “Things like reducing tariffs on select steel and aluminum products coming from China is something that might make the U.S. and not just Donald Trump, but also [U.S. Trade Representative] Jamieson Greer angry,” she suggests.
Steel, aluminum, and auto tariffs were among the major points of contention when U.S.-Canada trade negotiations broke down in August, with both sides accusing each other of walking back commitments.
Carney, however, has played down concerns that Canada's growing trade relationship with China is a major issue for Trump.
“In my conversation with the President, he’s tried to understand where we are with China, where we’re going with China,” said Carney during a news conference in Shenzhen. “I shouldn’t speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it’s not the top issue at all.”
Meanwhile, some Canadian officials have voiced concerns on expanding trade with China.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford warned Carney on Monday against opening the door for more Chinese-made EV vehicles in Canada, arguing the “government’s focus needs to be on protecting Canadian auto workers, not undermining them by importing even more state-subsidized cheap Chinese cars.”
Michael Chong, a lawmaker from Canada’s Conservative Party, during a press conference on Wednesday supported maintaining a dialogue with Beijing, but described Carney’s budding strategic partnership with China as a “risky gambit,” citing potential “national security” concerns.
In 2025, Ottawa identified China as one of the main perpetrators of foreign interference and espionage against Canada alongside other countries such as Russia and Iran. The Canadian government’s own analysis of Canada-China relations also points out that there are "associated risks” in broader trade cooperation in key areas, such as “prevalent and persistent intellectual property theft, and the risk of diversion of sensitive goods and technologies intended for civilian use for military purposes and applications.”
Carney said ahead of his Asia trip that he would raise concerns about foreign interference in his meeting with Xi. "The advantage of these meetings is you can raise issues directly and frankly,” he told reporters in Montreal on Nov. 10. Carney added that he would stress the importance Canada places on "the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries.”
In a press briefing during the APEC summit, Carney emphasized that Canada's trade with China is largely focused on commodities, rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors.
“We are exporting canola, we are exporting pork. We are exporting halibut,” Carney said , also citing liquefied natural gas and oil. “These are important industries. These are not cutting-edge semi-conductors.”
Experts point out that Canada could pursue deeper cooperation with other international partners in sectors where a closer relationship with China would be more difficult, including defense and advanced technology.
“[Canada] is not going to partner with China on defense, security, AI, and digital technology, things like that would be very difficult. [Carney] would have an impossible time trying to convince Canadians that's what we should be doing,” says Turnbull. “For those things, [Canada] would be putting [its] arms around the European Union.”
In September, the European Union unveiled its vision for Canada to become an “associate member” of the bloc. During an E.U.-Canada summit in Montreal in October, the two sides underscored their commitment to this plan, paving the way for deeper cooperation in areas including A
